The first calculation supplies the Eisenstein identity used in the pairing. The second supplies the numerator and denominator in the local factors of that pairing.

6.11Where the quotient volume comes from

Doubling puts the two copies of the source in a single hyperbolic space. There is a test vector Δ(Φ₁, Φ₂) on the doubled space whose kernel on the embedded pair (g₁, g₂) recovers the product of the original kernels. In the source’s orientation this product is χB(det g₂) times the doubled kernel. The Siegel–Weil section of Δ restricted to (g,1) gives W(g). Extending the section by the height contributes exactly h(g)s−s₀. The determinant character explains the inverse twist in the doubling integral. Doubled test vector and section[765] the integrand on the embedded group[766]

Siegel–Weil identifies the normalized mean of the doubled theta kernel with an Eisenstein value at s₀. For b ≤ 2a the proof invokes the convergent-range theorem with a + WittIndex(B) < b. For b > 2a, the series identity applies in the convergence region s₀ > a/2. When the two source integrals are paired, the squared norm of each kernel on the target grows at most polynomially. Cuspidal rapid decay makes the absolute triple integral finite, so the target pairing can be performed first. Converting the normalized target mean into the Petersson integral multiplies it by vol([H]). This produces a holomorphic continuation value of the full doubling integral. The proof first works at the frame lattice, then transfers it to the given self-dual lattice. the two Siegel–Weil ranges[767] the quotient volume in the seesaw identity[768] initial convergence and the continued value[769] transfer to a self-dual lattice[770]

When does the theta mean equal an Eisenstein value?

Doubling puts the two test vectors into one function φ on the space for the doubled source. Fix an element g of that group. There are now two ways to make a number. On the theta side, integrate the doubled kernel over the target quotient [H] and divide by its volume. On the Eisenstein side, form a section f from φ and sum its translates over rational cosets of the subgroup P stabilizing a maximal isotropic subspace of the doubled space. This subgroup is the Siegel parabolic. A complex parameter s varies the section and hence its sum E(g,s). The theorem supplies absolute integrability of the theta kernel for each g. Its second conclusion identifies the holomorphic value of the Eisenstein family at s₀.

E(g,s₀) = vol([H])−1 ∫[H] θφ(g,h) dh,   s₀ = (b − a)/2.

The chain uses ranks 1 ≤ a < b. Its hypotheses require the Witt index w of the target to be zero or satisfy a + w < b. They also specify the Weil action with characters 1 and χB on the doubled pair, the compatible compact subgroup and archimedean Cartan involutions, the polynomial Fock vector, the covolume-one normalization on the rational lattice and the target Haar measure. The factor vol([H]) returns when the pairing of the two lifts uses the integral of the kernel. Which value does the left side mean? The Eisenstein series converges absolutely in the open half-plane Re s > a/2. If b > 2a, then s₀ lies inside. The Weil–Siegel series formula identifies the sum at s₀ with the theta mean, and holomorphy of the flat family there identifies this sum with its holomorphic value. If a < b ≤ 2a, the rank and Witt conditions give a + w < b even in the branch w = 0. Here the convergent-range Siegel–Weil theorem supplies the integrable theta kernel and the value obtained by continuing the Eisenstein family. The underlying theta integral still converges. Its convergence and the region of absolute convergence of the Eisenstein series are two different statements. Construct the section and move between models. At s₀ the section f is built from the translate of φ by g. Restrict that function to pairs (v,−v) and integrate over a fundamental region for the rational lattice in v. For example, at the identity, the doubled test function Δ(Φ₁,Φ₂) restricts to Φ₁(v) Φ₂(v). Thus its section value there is the original inner product. To compute f(pg) write p ∈ P as a Levi block with matrix M times a unipotent element. The unipotent character is evaluated at zero and contributes 1. The Levi action contributes χB−1(det M) and the normalized absolute determinant to the power s₀ + a/2 = b/2. The compact translates of the Fock vector span a finite-dimensional space. Applying the linear section map to that space gives the same finiteness for the compact translates of f. To move away from s₀, multiply f(g) by the positive Siegel height h(g)s−s₀. It equals one as a multiplier on the compact subgroup, and increases the determinant exponent to s + a/2. In the range b ≤ 2a the proof changes coordinates to a standard Schrödinger model, in which the theta kernel is a sum of a Schwartz–Bruhat function over rational vectors. The chart and a translation put the chosen compact data into standard position and carry the Fock polynomial to a polynomial Gaussian at infinity. The individual theta kernels then agree at the corresponding group arguments, hence so do their means. The chart also identifies the rational parabolic cosets. The two choices of height give a factor Ds₀−s in the comparison of the flat sections, where D is a fixed positive absolute determinant. It is an entire function of s, equals 1 at s₀, and therefore preserves the continued value there. Where does the strict half-plane come from?

At the identity, let hγ be the positive height of a representative of a rational Siegel coset. The spherical section to be summed has magnitude hγT, with T = Re s + a/2. Arithmetic reduction assigns to each coset a tuple j of a nonnegative integers. For a base B > 1 and a constant C, its height is at most C B−∑j. For any fixed tuple the number of cosets in any finite sample with this label is at most C Ba∑j. Multiplying those bounds gives a bound for the whole label.

∑γ with label j hγT ≤ C1+T (Ba−T)∑j.

For T > a, summing over the tuple gives a product of a geometric series with common ratio Ba−T < 1. This bounds every finite subsum, establishing summability of the nonnegative spherical majorant. Iwasawa decomposition and the bound for the section on the compact subgroup transfer convergence to the flat section and its translates. The terms vary holomorphically in s through powers of positive heights. Choose a small vertical strip around the point, with both edges inside the half-plane. Each term is bounded in absolute value throughout the strip by the sum of its absolute values at the two endpoint real parts, since a positive height raised to a real exponent is monotone in that exponent. Both endpoint majorants are summable. The holomorphic terms therefore converge locally uniformly. Check the endpoint. At a = 3, b = 6 and w = 2, one has 3 + 2 < 6. But s₀ = 3/2 equals the boundary, T = 3, and the geometric ratio is 1. The continued-value argument supplies the equality at this point. Keeping a = 3 and w = 2 and raising b to 7 gives s₀ = 2 and T = 7/2. Now the ratio is B−1/2 and the convergent series supplies the value. At equality, deciding convergence of a particular series would require a separate estimate.

How many rational classes can share a height label?

The convergence estimate groups rational Siegel cosets by a tuple of nonnegative integers. Write n for the source rank (called a above), d for the number of real places of the totally real field F, and B = 4d. Fix a label μ = (μ₁,…,μn). Two counts enter. First one covers the unipotent matrix coordinate by finitely many centres at scales set by μ. Then one bounds how many cosets can use any one centre. Both bounds are uniform over μ. Where the label comes from. Choose a rational group representative of the coset q. Iwasawa decomposition writes it as pk, where p belongs to the Siegel parabolic and k lies in a fixed compact subgroup. A fixed change of coordinates, the Cayley transform, expresses p using an invertible n × n block β and a skew-Hermitian unipotent block. Let s be the idele equal to ½ at infinity and 1 at the finite places. Adelic lattice reduction gives a rational row change Δ, integer exponents ℓi and a matrix c with both c and c−1 in a fixed compact set. Δβ = diag(sℓ₁,…,sℓn) c,   μi = m₀ − ℓi.
Which rows form a basis, and why is each label nonnegative?

Over the CM field E, the module of integral rows Λ has underlying ℤ-rank n[E : ℚ]. The real-place reduction selects n rows in Λ independent over E. They form the rows of Δ and a basis of En. Their span over the ring of integers contains MΛ for a fixed positive integer M, and is contained in Λ. To see why the index can be controlled, multiply the selected rows by an integral basis of E to obtain n[E : ℚ] rows. Their Gram determinant is the determinant for an integral lattice basis times the square of the sublattice index. Comparing this identity with the product bound on the selected row lengths controls the index and keeps the dyadically rescaled row matrix away from singularity. At infinity the row lengths are scaled by powers of 2. Passing to the idele s reverses the sign of these exponents. Row span and lattice ranks[799] Independent lattice rows and dyadic scales[800] Gram determinants, the index and bounded inverse[801] Combining the finite and infinite coordinates[798]

There is a uniform m₀ for the compact set of entries in the remaining block. For sufficiently large k, a rational entry of the form skω, with ω in this compact set, must be zero. Indeed, all these dilates together lie in a compact set with only finitely many rational entries. Each nonzero rational entry has a nonzero infinite component, while the dilates tend uniformly to zero there. If ℓi exceeded m₀, all entries of the corresponding lower row of an invertible rational matrix would vanish. Hence ℓi ≤ m₀ for all rows. The normalized idele absolute value of s is B−1. The product formula removes the rational determinant factors, and the compact determinant factor is bounded. This gives the height estimate h(q) ≤ ChB−∑μᵢ. Choosing reduction data gives a label for each coset. Count the centres for a fixed label. At scalar depth k, subtract a rational element from an adele of F to put it in a fixed compact set. Bound its real components in absolute value by a nonnegative integer R. At each real place use the grid 2−kℤ between −R and R. Its integer numerators have exactly 2·2kR + 1 possibilities. Rounding leaves an error of size at most 2−k. The finite component stays in a fixed compact set. Across the d real places the number of scalar centres is bounded by C₀ bk, where b = 2d, C₀ = (2R + 1)d and B = b². Choose δ in E with conjugate −δ so that (1,δ) is an F-basis. A skew-Hermitian matrix S can be described by n² scalar adelic coordinates tij. Its (i,j) entry is (tij−tji) + δ(tij+tji). On the diagonal this is 2δtii. Off the diagonal the two ordered entries share two scalar coordinates. Cover tij at depth μi+μj. Its error then carries the factor corresponding to the left and right diagonal scalings. Combining the coordinate choices writes S as a rational matrix plus a centre y plus DμωDμ, where Dμ = diag(sμᵢ) and the entries of ω lie in a fixed compact set. The finite set Yμ of centres is the image of the product of the scalar grids. Its size is at most the number of grid tuples. |Yμ| ≤ ∏i,j C₀ bμᵢ+μⱼ = C₀n² b2n∑μᵢ = C₀n² Bn∑μᵢ.

A rank-two count. Take one real place, a scalar grid with R = 1 and label μ = (1,0). The four ordered depths are 2, 1, 1 and 0. The corresponding lists of integer numerators have 9, 5, 5 and 3 entries. Their product gives 675 tuples. The formula above permits 3⁴·4² = 1,296. These numbers count candidates and bound their image. Counting rational cosets still requires the multiplicity argument.

Why a centre has bounded multiplicity. Subtract the rational unipotent term and put the compact error into a matrix w(q). In the Cayley coordinates the proof obtains a rational invertible matrix Z(q) = z(μ,y)w(q), with w(q) in a fixed compact set. The map q ↦ Z(q) is injective. In fact, equality of two such matrices makes the original rational representatives differ on the left by an element stabilizing the diagonal subspace. They represent the same Siegel coset. Removing the rational unipotent translation[812] Injectivity of the normalized rational matrix[813] The Siegel cosets in the application[790]

Fix μ and a centre y. For a nonempty finite collection of cosets using them, choose one member q₀. Multiplying by Z(q₀)−1 cancels the common left factor z(μ,y). The relative matrices w(q₀)−1w(q) are rational and belong to a fixed compact set, independent of μ, y and q₀. Each matrix entry belongs to a finite set of rational points, so there are at most N possible relative matrices. Left multiplication preserves injectivity. Each chosen centre can therefore account for at most N cosets. Summing over all available centres gives an upper bound even when some centres are unused and others occur for multiple cosets. A uniform bound for a fixed translate[814] Counting the fibre by its image[815]

#{q ∈ A with label μ} ≤ N |Yμ| ≤ N C₀n² Bn∑μᵢ   for every finite sample A.

A uniform finite bound on all finite samples also bounds the full fibre, since a larger fibre would contain a finite sample exceeding it. The summability proof uses exactly the finite-sample statement. Multiplication by the height bound raised to the power T gives the geometric decay when T > n. How do the Fourier coefficients recover the theta mean?

Consider the lower range of the Siegel–Weil formula. Write n for the source rank and m for the dimension of the target Hermitian space V over the quadratic extension E/F. Thus n < m ≤ 2n and n + WittIndex(V) < m. The evaluation point s₀ = (m − n)/2 can lie on the boundary of absolute convergence or to its left. Take a test function Φ in the global Fock subspace of the Schrödinger model. With this input we can compare one frequency of the two sides at a time. The frequencies are rational Hermitian n × n matrices β. A frequency is nondegenerate when det β ≠ 0. The range and the standard data[816] The exact full-rank conclusion[817]

For an automorphic function F, move g by the upper unipotent matrix u(b) with diagonal blocks 1 and upper right block b. Invariance under rational unipotent translations makes this function of b periodic. Its domain is the Hermitian adelic matrices modulo the rational ones. Use a fundamental region 𝒟 of volume one. Put ⟨β,b⟩ = ½ TrE/F(tr(βb)), with rational entries embedded in the adeles and the field trace extended to the adeles. The sign of the Fourier character[818]

Cβ(F)(g) = ∫𝒟 F(u(b)g) ψ(−⟨β,b⟩) db.

On the theta side, a frequency selects a Gram matrix. Write φ = ω(g)Φ for the translated test function. A rational tuple x of n vectors of V contributes φ(h−1x) to the theta kernel. Translating by u(b) multiplies this summand by ψ(⟨Gram(x),b⟩). The target action of h preserves the Gram matrix. After weighting by the inverse β-character, integration gives 1 if Gram(x) = β and 0 otherwise. Absolute theta convergence justifies grouping tuples by Gram matrix, averaging over [U(V)] and integrating the resulting character series. When det β ≠ 0, every tuple in that fibre has rank n, since rank(x∗Gram(V)x) ≤ rank(x). Thus Cβ(I)(g) is the normalized average of the sum over precisely these full-rank tuples, where I is the theta mean. The unipotent action on each summand[819] The Gram matrix and its rank[820] Absolute convergence and the Gram expansion[821] Integrating the characters term by term[822]

On the Eisenstein side, the same frequency selects the open cell. For Re z > n/2 the coset sum has a summable bound on a compact set of representatives. This permits integration of the sum by cells. On each other cell, when det β ≠ 0, there is a translation preserving its contribution and multiplying its character by a scalar different from 1. Its integral is therefore zero. The open-cell cosets are indexed by rational Hermitian translations. Their translates of 𝒟 cover the full adelic Hermitian space, giving the integral below. Here w is the Weyl element interchanging the two isotropic coordinate spaces and fz is the flat section. The open-cell parametrization and majorant[823] Cancellation on the other cells[824]

Cβ(E(·,z))(g) = ∫Hermn(𝔸) fz(w u(b)g) ψ(−⟨β,b⟩) db.

The Weyl action is a Fourier transform. Evaluating it at zero integrates the translated test function against the Gram character. Consequently the section in this integral is the Gram-character integral of φ times the height H(w u(b)g)z−s₀. This identifies the unfolded family on the right half-plane with the Whittaker integral for β. Its holomorphic value at s₀ is the same full-rank fibre average computed on the theta side. The input used here combines finite-place factors, the unramified Gram-density calculation, a real-place computation, global factorization and a low-rank density identity. Finite linear combination treats the compact argument, then the Iwasawa decomposition transports the identity to arbitrary g. What can be invisible to all the nondegenerate coefficients?

Take the additive group of symmetric 2 × 2 matrices over the field of three elements. This finite example has 27 elements. Set ζ = exp(2πi/3), T = diag(1,0) and F(B) = ζB₁₁. The normalized β-coefficient is the average of ζtr((T−β)B). At β = T all 27 terms are 1. For β ≠ T, at least one of the three matrix coordinates has a nonzero coefficient in this linear form. Its sum is 1 + ζ + ζ² = 0. The off-diagonal entry appears with multiplier 2, which is invertible in this field. Hence every invertible β has coefficient zero, although F(0) = 1. The missing information sits at the rank-one frequency T.

How does the proof rule out such a discrepancy? At a real place selected using the Witt-index inequality, choose a compactly supported test function η whose Fourier transform vanishes on singular Hermitian matrices. Suppose a continuous automorphic function F has zero full-rank coefficients for all g. Integrate its unipotent translates against η. The β-coefficient of this convolution factors into the β-coefficient of F and the transform of η at the associated local frequency. For invertible β the first factor is zero. For singular β the associated local matrix is singular too, so the second factor is zero. All Fourier coefficients of the convolution now vanish, so Fourier uniqueness on the compact Hermitian quotient makes the convolution zero. Density and continuity give the same vanishing with a group translation on either side of the unipotent argument. Removing a possible pole and computing the value

At this real place, first take the Gaussian Fock vector (the constant polynomial 1). The local signature condition gives a choice of η and of the two translations for which a compact-group average defines an operator T with nonzero scalar c(0) on the theta mean of this vector. On the corresponding regularized Eisenstein family the scalar is c(z−s₀). Meanwhile, the convolution argument shows that T kills every automorphic discrepancy with zero full-rank coefficients. On a discrepancy with eigenvalue c(0), this forces the discrepancy itself to vanish. The detector and its nonzero scalar[835] The regularized family and both eigenrelations[836] The use of the nondegenerate functionals[837]

To see where holomorphy enters, write the continued Eisenstein family as A(z)/d(z) with holomorphic numerator and polynomial denominator. Factor d(z) = (z−s₀)kd₁(z) with d₁(s₀) ≠ 0. The full-rank coefficient identities ensure that while a power remains in the denominator, the regularized numerator at the point has zero full-rank coefficients. Its eigenvalue forces that value to vanish, so one can divide the numerator by z−s₀ holomorphically and repeat. After k divisions, the difference between the resulting numerator at s₀ and d₁(s₀)I is killed by T and has eigenvalue c(0). It is zero. Division by d₁ now gives the required value. The argument extends from the Gaussian to polynomial Fock vectors through the local Fock operators and their generation of the polynomial sections. The standard-model result supplies the lower branch of the doubled formula after the change of model. Holomorphic value at z = s₀ of E(g,z) = I(g).
What does a full-rank Whittaker factor count at a good finite place?

The open-cell integral compares a Fourier coefficient of the Eisenstein series with the mean of tuples of vectors having Gram matrix T. At a good finite place v, this comparison has a concrete arithmetic content. Count the tuples whose Gram matrix agrees with T modulo increasing powers of a uniformizer. Once the measures are fixed, the normalized count gives the local Whittaker value at z₀ = (M−n)/2, where M is the dimension of the Hermitian space and n is the number of vectors.

Write q for the size of the residue field of Fv. At the places treated here, 2 is a unit, the local quadratic algebra is unramified, the forms J and T are integral with unit determinant, and the scalar character ψv has conductor the valuation ring. The integral lattice is trace-self-dual. Set ε = −1 when the quadratic algebra is the unramified field, and ε = +1 when it splits. The Schwartz function is the characteristic function of the integral M × n matrix lattice. A nonzero rational det T gives this unit condition at almost all places. Count one Gram fibre. Let Nk be the number of distinct matrices X modulo ϖk satisfying X∗JX ≡ T. Here ∗ is conjugate transpose. There are q2kMn possible input matrices and qkn² Hermitian targets. The density compares the proportion of matrices in this fibre with the proportion one would obtain if every target occurred equally often. The finite-level density[850] Counting solutions and normalizing the counts[851]

αk(J,T) = Nk · qkn²/q2kMn = ∏j=0n−1 (1 − (ε/q)M−j),   k ≥ 1,   n ≤ M.

At level one a change of basis reduces the unimodular target to the identity. Solutions are orthonormal frames over the residue algebra. Choose one vector of norm one, then choose the next in its orthogonal complement. In dimension r, the norm-one count is q2r−1(1−(ε/q)r). The successive dimensions M, …, M−n+1 give the product above after normalization. Why does the density stay constant at deeper levels?

Lift a solution modulo ϖk by writing its next representative as X+ϖkY. For k ≥ 1 the quadratic term in Y disappears modulo ϖk+1. The correction must solve the linear equation Y∗JX+X∗JY = H in the residue algebra, with H Hermitian. It is solvable for every H. For instance, since 2 and T are invertible here, take Y = ½XT−1H. The linear map has a domain with q2Mn elements and a codomain with qn² elements. Every fibre has q2Mn−n² elements. Thus Nk+1 gains exactly the factor cancelled by the next density normalization. A Gram fibre over nine elements. Take ℚ(i) over ℚ at the inert prime 3, J = I₃ and T = I₂. Then q = 3 and ε = −1. In 𝔽₉ the norm of a+bi is a²+b² in 𝔽₃. There are 252 choices for a norm-one column of length three. For each, its two-dimensional orthogonal complement has 24 norm-one columns. This gives 6,048 frames among 9⁶ matrices at the first level. The normalized density is 6,048/3⁸ = 224/243 = (1+3−3)(1−3−2). Each frame has 3⁸ lifts to level two.

Which integral gives this number? Use the self-dual Haar measure on the matrix space for its Weil pairing and the self-dual Haar measure on the Hermitian matrices for their trace pairing. Write ⟨T,b⟩ for half the quadratic-algebra trace of tr(Tb). The source integrates the following expression in b. Inside it the character has positive Gram phase, and the Fourier projection contributes the negative target phase. The height is h(b) = vol(L+bL)/vol(L) for the standard column lattice L. The auxiliary Haar measure in this ratio cancels. Wv(z) = ∫ h(b)−(z−z₀) ψv(−⟨T,b⟩) (∫integral X ψv(⟨b,X∗JX⟩) dX) db,   Re z > n².

At a good place the Hermitian integral lattice has volume one. Grouping by its cosets rewrites the integral as a sum. The cosets appear in increasing finite sets indexed by a level k. With t = εMq−(2z+n), their sums of absolute values have a geometric majorant because qn²|t| < 1 in the stated half-plane. Each positive-level sum is the same polynomial in t. How do congruence counts determine a polynomial?

At each positive level the finite Fourier sum is a polynomial Pk(t) whose terms are weighted by the level character at the negative target, and by a nonnegative lattice-index exponent of t. Evaluate it at t = (ε/q)m for each auxiliary rank m ≥ n. Finite Fourier orthogonality and the Gaussian sums identify that evaluation with the density of T for the identity form in dimension m. The counting formula just proved gives ∏j(1−(ε/q)m−j). This equals the evaluation of ∏j(1−t(εq)j) at the same point. Those points have distinct absolute values, so the two polynomials agree everywhere. The auxiliary rank varies only in this interpolation step. Wv(z) = ∏j=0n−1 (1−εM+jq−(2z+n−j)),   Wv(z₀) = α₁(J,T).

The product extends to an entire function of z. Substituting 2z₀ = M−n gives exactly the density, since εM+j = εM−j. In the example z₀ = ½, while the integral theorem assumes Re z > 4. The continued value is therefore obtained by evaluating the explicit product. From places to the global coefficient. The pure adelic datum is standard outside a finite set. The comparison then returns through Iwasawa decomposition and the open-cell identity to the coefficient at every group argument. What replaces the good-place formula at an exceptional finite place?

The good-place count assumes a particular test function, the indicator of the full matrix lattice. A test supported on just one residue class can change the answer even at an unramified prime. The local argument works at every finite place and gives an entire function of the complex parameter z. Its value at s₀ = (M−n)/2 is the density of the chosen test at the target Gram matrix. The global application has n < M. The local statement used in assembly[878] The rank-independent local construction[879]

Fix the local quadratic algebra Ev = Fv ⊗F E, the local component ψv of the adelic additive character, a nondegenerate Hermitian form J of rank M, and a Hermitian target T of size n whose determinant is invertible in Ev. This allows determinants of nonzero valuation. A test Φ is a locally constant, compactly supported function of the M × n matrix X. Use the self-dual measures μ on the matrix space and ν on the Hermitian space for their respective pairings. For a Haar measure λ on Evn and two compact open additive subgroups L₁, L₂, put r(b) = λ(L₁+bL₂)/λ(L₁). It is at least one. Write ⟨b,S⟩ for half the field-algebra trace of the matrix trace of bS. The opposite signs single out the fibre X∗JX = T. u(b) = ∫ Φ(X) ψv(⟨b,X∗JX−T⟩) dμ(X),   Wv(z) = ∫ r(b)−(z−s₀) u(b) dν(b)   for Re z sufficiently large.

Why can one compact ball determine an entire function? On a shell R < ‖b‖ ≤ 2R, change variables by b ↦ (1+x)∗b(1+x), with x in a small additive matrix ball of radius C/R. These changes preserve the shell, its Haar measure, the lattice index and the integral containing the positive Gram phase. The negative target phase acquires a term linear in x and a term quadratic in x. The latter has norm bounded by a constant times R(C/R)², so the character is trivial on it for large R. Invertibility of T lets one choose C so that at every b in the shell the linear term gives a nontrivial character of the x-ball. Its Haar integral is zero. Averaging the change of variables therefore kills the shell integral for every z, with one cutoff valid for all z. At a singular target the linear term can lose this oscillation, and the stated density hypothesis covers only the regular set. Choose a ball B₀ beyond that cutoff and double its radius successively. Adding any of the resulting shells leaves the integral over B₀ unchanged. On B₀ the index and its logarithm are bounded, so one can differentiate the compact integral with respect to z. This gives an entire Wv, with no poles. A separate absolute estimate identifies it with the original integral on a right half-plane. For radii growing by a fixed local dilation, the jth outer shell has r(b) ≥ 2j and volume at most a constant times κj. Thus the integral of the absolute value has a geometric majorant when Re z is large. The statement requires existence of a real threshold depending on the data. Integrating over a large additive ball Λ in b retains those X whose Gram matrix belongs to T+Λ⊥. Indeed, the average of the phase on Λ is one when the difference annihilates Λ and zero otherwise. The annihilator shrinks into the regular set around T, and self-duality gives ν(Λ)ν(Λ⊥) = 1. The integral is therefore an average of g near T. By continuity it approaches g(T). ∫Λ u(b) dν(b) = (1/ν(Λ⊥)) ∫T+Λ⊥ g(S) dν(S)   ⟶   g(T) = Wv(s₀).
Compute the entire factor for one residue class at 3

Take E = ℚ(i), F = ℚ and the inert prime 3. Let J be the two-dimensional identity, n = 1, T = 1 and L₁ = L₂ = 𝒪Eᵥ. Use a character of conductor ℤ₃. The standard integral lattices have self-dual volume one here. Let Φ be the indicator of X ≡ (1,0) modulo 3. There are four scalar coordinates over ℤ₃, so this class has mass 1/81. Its Gram value N(X₁)+N(X₂) belongs to 1+3ℤ₃. For each lift to the next power of 3, the derivative in the real coordinate of X₁ is 2 modulo 3. For each choice of the other three digits, exactly one digit of this coordinate gives the required next Gram digit. Thus the mass is uniform on 1+3ℤ₃, a set of volume 1/3, and the density there is 1/27.

Integration of the character on this coset, including the negative target phase, gives u(b) = (1/81) · 𝟙3⁻¹ℤ₃(b). On ℤ₃ the lattice index is one. On the shell 3⁻¹ℤ₃ ∖ ℤ₃, of volume two, its value is nine because the residue field of Ev has nine elements. In this example the original integral has compact support and converges at every z.

W₃(z) = (1 + 2 · 9−(z−1/2))/81,   W₃(1/2) = 1/27.

Now keep J = I₂ and T = 1, and restore the full-lattice test. There are 24 norm-one columns modulo 3. At every such column at least one scalar derivative of the norm is nonzero modulo 3, so each residue class contributes the same density 1/27. Summing the 24 contributions gives 24/27 = 8/9, the good-place answer in these same dimensions.

Which domain reaches the global coefficient? The local proof uses no rank inequality to construct the entire function once a density is given. The global theorem supplies these densities from the normalized Gram mean when n < M and either n+2 ≤ M or J is anisotropic. It chooses a finite set S outside which the forms, measures, lattices and test meet the good-place conditions. On Re z > 0 multiply the archimedean function, the finitely many entire factors Wv for v ∈ S, and the convergent good-place product. Farther right this equals the adelic integral for the full-rank Fourier coefficient. The point s₀ lies inside the global half-plane by the strict rank inequality. Substituting the local density values gives the normalized Gram mean there. The resulting global continuation is holomorphic on Re z > 0. Why does a product of local Gram densities give a global mean?

At one finite place a density measures how often a tuple has a prescribed Gram matrix. A rational tuple must satisfy the same equations at every place. To bring these two descriptions together the proof averages over all adelic isometries of a single rational Hermitian space. Let E/F be the CM extension, J the nondegenerate Hermitian form on EM, and T a rational nonsingular Hermitian matrix of size n. The theorem assumes n < M, with either n+2 ≤ M or J anisotropic over E. Anisotropic means that a rational vector of norm zero must itself be zero. The test Φ has a Schwartz factor at infinity and locally constant, compactly supported factors at finite places. Almost all finite factors are the characteristic function of the standard lattice. At every place the two Hermitian matrices come from these same rational forms, and each local additive character comes from one global character. Replacing h by γh for a rational isometry γ permutes these solutions by X ↦ γ−1X. The sum therefore defines a function on the quotient. Integrate it over 𝒟 using Haar measure and divide by vol(𝒟). Equivalently one can first add the measures obtained by moving each rational tuple under h ↦ h−1X, normalizing their sum by the same volume, then integrate Φ. Why can grouping the terms change their weights?

A finite group makes the Haar weights visible. Take H to be the six permutations of three letters and put Γ = K = {id,(12)}. A function constant on ΓhK has just two values. The class of the identity contains two permutations. The class of (13) contains the remaining four. Indeed the size of ΓhK is |Γ||K|/|Γ ∩ hKh−1|, and the two intersection sizes are 2 and 1. If the function takes values 2 and 5, the normalized Haar average is (2·2 + 4·5)/6 = 4. Giving both classes weight ½ would give 3½. The same issue arises when a quotient integral is grouped into classes, whose weights come from their volumes. The definition above keeps that weighting by integrating on a fundamental domain.

Build the global measure one vector at a time. A tuple with no columns has one possible value. For a positive number of columns choose a rational vector of nonzero length t in the target form T. A change of basis writes T as the orthogonal sum of the line ⟨t⟩ and a nonsingular form T₁. If J represents t over E, choose such a vector and split J into the same line and a complement J₁. After fixing the first vector, the remaining columns lie in its orthogonal complement and have Gram matrix T₁. Both dimensions have dropped by one. This preserves the gap M−n. In the boundary case M = n+1 the complement of an anisotropic form is still anisotropic. Why can we integrate the paired kernels in either order?

Let X = [G] be the source quotient and Y = [H] the target quotient, with their quotient Haar measures μ and ν. Each is the space of adelic points modulo rational changes of basis. Bound one kernel at a time. Take the same polynomial Φ on both sides of the doubled kernel. The height at (g,g) is at most a constant times a power of the height at g. Multiplying the mean by ν(Y) therefore gives a polynomial bound for ∫Y |K(g,y)|² dν(y). The restriction to the compact stabilizer would contribute just c(1), since the integrand is constant there and its volume is one. Freeing the local variable multiplies that contribution by the displayed quotient. The denominator therefore enters once each time a good place is freed.

The numerator runs over every CM place w above v and every Satake parameter β there. Its factor is (1 − β χB(w)−1 Nw−(s+½))−1, where χB(w) denotes the unramified character value. The actual step vector starts with a nonzero Fock vacuum f. Let I₀ be its squared norm in the chosen covolume-one pairing. The sum runs over cosets gKn. With n = m + 2, write Gm for the smaller unitary group and U for the upper block triangular unitary matrices with identity diagonal blocks of sizes 1, m, 1. ℤ × (Gm/Km) × (U/(U ∩ Kn))   →   Gn/Kn,   (a, g₀Km, [u]) ↦ MuKn.

Changing u by an integral factor on the right leaves its image unchanged. Changing the chosen representative for the middle coset can change the radical coordinate. Test the distinction between a coset and a double coset. Over ℚ₃(i), in rank two, take M₊ = diag(3, 1/3) and M₋ = diag(1/3, 3). Let Cj count radical cosets of length at most H + j. The lattice length test permits row denominators at level e = a₊ + ⌊j/2⌋ and a corrected upper corner at level f = 2a₊ + j. The number of row classes is q2(h+me). Each of the m row coordinates uses the extension residue field of size q², and the fixed middle lattice accounts for h. Every admissible row lifts because 2e ≤ f. With a row fixed, the difference between any two corners has trace zero. There are qf classes of such differences modulo integral ones. Multiplying the two counts gives

Cj = c q2m⌊j/2⌋+j,   c = q2h+(2m+2)a₊.

Three steps explain the count. The length calculation for one matrix derives the two levels e and f. At those levels, the row calculation counts the admissible rows and constructs a lift of each one. The trace-zero calculation counts the corners above that lift. The counting proof chooses a lift of each row and constructs a bijection with the product of the row and trace-zero quotients. How the length of one matrix determines the two levels

Length counts independent denominators in the lattice generated by the standard rows and the rows of the given matrix. Fix the signed outer valuation a, a middle unitary block g of size m and length h, and one unipotent representative with row r, paired column b and upper corner c. In three blocks their product has the form

G = diag(ϖa, g, ϖ−a) · [(1, r, c), (0, I, b), (0, 0, 1)],

where the three parenthesized triples are block rows. The middle lattice supplies integral matrices U,V,C with gC integral, (U + Vg)C = I and v(det C) = h. We use the additive valuation v(ϖ) = 1. For any scalar or row x, let d(x) be the least integer k ≥ 0 for which ϖkx is integral in every coordinate. This includes d(0) = 0. Put

α = max(a,0),   R = d(rC),   S = d(c − r · (CVg)b),   t = max(0,R − α).

The length of G is |a| + h + max(2t, S − 2α). Thus a budget of j above |a| + h allows R ≤ α + ⌊j/2⌋ and S ≤ 2α + j, simultaneously. For a ≥ 0 the allowable levels are e = a + ⌊j/2⌋ and f = 2a + j. For a < 0, the base length still includes −a but the two levels are just ⌊j/2⌋ and j. Derive the length by eliminating rows

In the sum of the two row lattices, combine the middle rows of the identity using U and the middle rows of G using V. These mixed rows form the block (0, C−1, Vgb). Multiplying this block on the left by C and subtracting the standard middle rows leaves pure last coordinates (CVg)b. Likewise, subtracting gC times the mixed rows from the middle rows of G leaves (gCU)b. The original last rows also give the scalars 1 and ϖ−a. The pure last coordinates just listed span the fractional ideal generated by y = ϖ−α−t. Indeed the row and column identity says that a power of ϖ clears rC exactly when it clears both columns (CVg)b and (gCU)b. The largest denominator among those columns, 1 and ϖ−a thus needs α + t powers, and some generator attains that value. Build a triangular block matrix P with these mixed middle rows and last row (0,0,y). For a ≥ 0 keep the first standard row in P and subtract ϖa times it from the first row of G. For a < 0 keep the first row of G and subtract the first standard row from ϖ−a times the retained row. Either way the extra row is (0,ϖαr,ϖαc). The pivot in the first column of P is 1 in the first case and ϖa in the second. The other diagonal blocks are C−1 and y, so −v(det P) = max(−a,0) + h + α + t = |a| + h + t. In the basis of rows of P, the coordinates of the extra row are

ρ = (0, ϖαrC, ϖα(c − r · (CVg)b)/y).

The middle term already contributes ϖαr · (CVg)b in the last column, explaining the subtraction. The largest denominator exponent in ρ is t′ = max(t, S − 2α − t). If t′ is zero, the extra row already belongs to the lattice of P. Otherwise replace a row of P whose coefficient in ρ has valuation −t′ with the extra row. The new determinant is the old determinant times that coefficient. The old row is recovered by dividing by this same coefficient, since its inverse and the ratios of every other coefficient to it are integral. This gives a basis of the full enlarged lattice. Its length is |a| + h + t + t′, the formula above. Equal entry valuations, different lengths. Work over ℚ₃(i), with i² = −1 and conjugation σ(i) = −i. The residue field is 𝔽₉. In both cases rC = (1,1) and r · (CVg)b = −1/3. The corrected corners are 0 and i/3. The formula gives lengths 1 and 2.

One can also count directly modulo the standard lattice. The third row of G is (0,0,1/3,−1/3). After subtracting this row and the first two standard basis vectors from the first row of G, the only remaining entry is c + 1/3 in the last column. The other rows of G are integral. Thus the first matrix adds one residue-field direction. The second adds that same direction and the independent vector (0,0,0,i/3). The respective quotients have 9 and 81 elements. Either column can supply the largest denominator

Over ℚ₃(i) with i² = −1 and σ(i) = −i, take the matrices below. Each pair of parentheses denotes one row.

g = [(1, i/3), (0, 1)],   C = diag(1,3),   U = [(1,0), (i,0)],   V = [(0,0), (−i,0)].

The upper-right entry of g has trace zero, so σ(g)TJg = J. Multiplication gives U + Vg = diag(1,1/3) and gC = [(1,i),(0,3)]. Both CVg and gCU have zero first row. Their last rows are (−3i,1) and (3i,0). For r = (1/3,i/9) the paired column is b = (i/9,−1/3)T. The last entries of w,z are 1/3 − 1/3 = 0 and −1/3. Change just the second row coordinate to i/3. Counting the rows and lifting each one

The row count has to answer two questions. How many row classes pass the lattice test? For each such row, is there a corner with the required denominator that makes the matrix unitary? Fix the middle unitary block g of size m and length h. The lattice calculation supplies integral matrices U,V,C with gC integral, (U + Vg)C = I and v(det C) = h. Here v is additive with v(ϖ) = 1. At row level e, set A = ϖeC. The admissible rows form Λ = {r ∈ Lm : rA ∈ 𝒪m}, and two rows have the same class when their difference is integral. Write A = P diag(ϖd₁,…,ϖdₘ) Q with P,Q and their inverses integral. The diagonal matrix is integral because it equals P−1AQ−1, so every dᵢ ≥ 0. Changing r to rP preserves the integral row lattice and removes P from the calculation. Multiplying on the right by Q preserves integrality in both directions. The ith coordinate can now range over ϖ−dᵢ𝒪/𝒪. This quotient has (q²)dᵢ elements, since each digit ranges over the extension residue field. Multiplying the coordinate counts and taking determinants gives

[Λ : 𝒪m] = (q²)∑ dᵢ = (q²)v(det A) = q2(h+me).

Raising the row level by one allows one additional residue-field digit in each of the m coordinates. The factor (q²)h is already present at level zero. How to choose the corner

For a representative r ∈ Λ, form its paired column b by bᵢ = −σ(rm+1−i), using indices 1 through m. Put b₁ = CVg b and b₂ = CU b, where these subscripts now label two whole vectors. They add to b since C(U + Vg) = I. The lattice duality calculation gives ϖeb₁ and ϖeg b₂ integral. To see where g enters, expand r = (rC)U + ((rC)V)g. Negating, conjugating and reversing coordinates sends this to b = x + g−1y with ϖex and ϖey integral, by unitarity of g. Thus b₁ = (I − CU)x + CVy and g b₂ = gCUx + (I − gCV)y. Both expressions have integral matrix coefficients. Why the scaled row bounds two columns[1118] Splitting the paired column[1126]

Write ⟨x,y⟩ = ∑ᵢ σ(xᵢ)ym+1−i for the Hermitian form and Tr(z) = z + σ(z). Choose an integral τ with Tr(τ) = 1. For example, τ = σ(z)/(σ(z) − z) works whenever z is integral and its difference from its conjugate is a unit. Put

s = ⟨b₁,b₁⟩ − ⟨b₂,b₂⟩,   c = r · b₁ + τs.

The two norms make s fixed by σ. Since r · b₁ = −⟨b,b₁⟩, the trace of c is −⟨b,b₁⟩ − ⟨b₁,b⟩ + s = −⟨b,b⟩ = r · b. This is precisely the unitary relation on the upper-right entry of the unipotent matrix with row r and column b. Its corrected corner is c − r · b₁ = τs. Multiplying a Hermitian norm by ϖ2e scales each of its two arguments by ϖe. For the second norm use ⟨b₂,b₂⟩ = ⟨gb₂,gb₂⟩. Both scaled norms are integral. Consequently the corrected corner passes the test at every f ≥ 2e. The ball count takes e = max(a,0) + ⌊j/2⌋ and f = 2 max(a,0) + j, so every row in its index actually lifts. A row that uses both denominator powers. Over ℚ₂(ω) with ω² + ω + 1 = 0, take m = 1, g = C = U = 1 and V = 0. With a = 1 and j = 0 the levels are e = 1, f = 2. The four row classes in ½𝒪/𝒪 are represented by 0, 1/2, ω/2 and (1 + ω)/2. Choose r = 1/2. Then b = −1/2, b₁ = 0, b₂ = b, and s = −1/4. Taking τ = −ω gives Tr(τ) = 1 and c = ω/4. Indeed 4c is integral and Tr(c) = −1/4. At the hypothetical smaller level f = 1, any lift of this row would need 2c integral while Tr(2c) = −1/2. Why one more corner digit gives q choices

Fix an admissible row in a unitary cell. Its paired column is then fixed, and the upper-right entry c satisfies c + σ(c) = row · column. Two lifts of the same row therefore differ in the corner by an element of trace zero. Subtracting their corrected corner conditions cancels the row–column term and says that ϖf times this difference is integral. For the valuation ring 𝒪, put T = {u ∈ 𝒪 : σ(u) = −u}. After choosing one lift, all the allowable differences form ϖ−fT. An integral change of corner contributes an element of T, so the fiber over this row class has size [ϖ−fT : T]. The row, column and corrected corner condition[1077] How a change of corner acts within a fixed row[1131] The product of row and corner quotients[1132] The corner theorem in the spherical integral[1096] The named supplier[1133]

The residue field 𝒪/ϖ𝒪 has q² elements. To compute the number of its digits available in a trace-zero corner, choose x ∈ 𝒪 such that Δ = σ(x) − x is a unit. Its existence is part of the unramified involution hypotheses. Every y ∈ 𝒪 has two integral trace-zero coordinates

u = σ(x)y − xσ(y),   w = σ(y) − y,   y = (u + xw)/Δ.

Conversely, start from any u,w ∈ T and use the last formula for y. Since σ(Δ) = −Δ, one gets σ(y) = (u + σ(x)w)/Δ, which recovers w and then u. Thus this is an additive isomorphism T × T ≃ 𝒪. It commutes with multiplication by ϖ because σ fixes ϖ. Reducing both sides modulo ϖ gives [T : ϖT]² = |𝒪/ϖ𝒪| = q². In particular every corner digit has q choices. This proof works even in residue characteristic two because its only scalar division is by the unit Δ. Multiplication by ϖf identifies the original quotient with T/ϖfT. Each successive quotient ϖiT/ϖi+1T is isomorphic to T/ϖT, so there are precisely qf corner classes, including one when f = 0. The counting theorem inserts this as the second factor, alongside the separate row-lattice index. It uses f = 2 max(a,0) + j in the ball of excess length j. Four corners at level two. Take L = ℚ₂(ω), where ω² + ω + 1 = 0. This polynomial is irreducible and separable modulo 2, giving the unramified quadratic extension with 𝒪 = ℤ₂[ω], ϖ = 2 and q = 2. Here σ(ω) = −1 − ω. The trace of a + bω is 2a − b, so T = ℤ₂η with η = 1 + 2ω. Taking x = ω gives Δ = −η, a unit. With row zero the column and its correction vanish. At f = 2 the corners have representatives 0, η/4, η/2 and 3η/4. Each has integral quadruple and trace zero. Two representatives agree modulo T precisely when their numerators in units of η agree modulo 4. This checks the local index even in residue characteristic two. In the global chain every dyadic place outside the exceptional set must split. This inert dyadic example therefore illustrates the local counting lemma only. 6.19Pass from balls to shells

For j = 2k, substitution in the count gives C2kX2k = c(y²)k, since y = qm+1X. For j = 2k + 1 the row level stays fixed and the corner gains one level. Its term therefore gains the factor qX. Adding the two geometric series gives c(1 + qX)/(1 − y²). A coset of length H + 2 occurs in every ball with j ≥ 2. To count it exactly once, subtract the preceding ball. The shell counts are d₀ = C₀ and dj = Cj − Cj−1 for j ≥ 1. Subtracting the shifted series multiplies by 1 − X. Restoring the length offset gives

∑j≥0 djXH+j = c XHJm(X),   Jm(X) = (1 − X)(1 + qX)/(1 − y²).

Taking |X| in the same shell calculation proves absolute convergence. It authorizes regrouping individual cosets by length. Even and odd series[1139] first differences[1140] absolute convergence over all radical cosets[1141]

A cell in rank three. Set m = 1, q = 3, a = h = 0. The first four balls contain 1, 3, 81 and 243 cosets. The shells therefore contain 1, 2, 78 and 162. At X = 1/27, y = 1/3, their infinite weighted sum is (26/27)(10/9)/(8/9) = 65/54. The value 65/54 accounts for the diagonal label a = 0 alone. To obtain the local Euler factor, the sum over diagonal valuations weights each cell by its spherical coefficient and includes every a ∈ ℤ.

6.20Sum the positive and negative diagonal valuations

Let β be the first Satake parameter and φ₀ the normalized induced function for the remaining parameters. On the block with labels a, g₀, spherical induction contributes βaq−a(m+1)φ₀(g₀). Multiply this by the shell sum just found. The identity 2a₊ − a = |a| groups the factors into the following product.

Jm(X) · βay|a| · (q²X)hφ₀(g₀).

For a ≥ 0 the middle piece sums to 1/(1 − yβ). For a < 0 it starts at y/β and sums to (y/β)/(1 − y/β). Bringing these to a common denominator gives numerator 1 − y². This cancels the same denominator in Jm. Write Zn for the full normalized spherical sum and α′ for the tail of the parameter list. Summing the third piece over g₀Km now gives the smaller rank sum, with X replaced by q²X.

Zm+2(X,y;β,α′) = [(1 − X)(1 + qX)/((1 − yβ)(1 − y/β))] · Zm(q²X,y;α′).

The hypotheses on |yβ| and |y/β| guarantee both sums converge. In ranks zero and one the whole unitary group is integral, so the normalized sum is 1. The two valuation series and separation of the smaller sum[1142] small-rank base cases[1143] application of the recurrence to the unitary cosets[1144]

6.21Read off the normalizing factor

Every rank reduction extracts the pair (1 − yβ)−1(1 − y/β)−1. The successive choices X, q²X, … give the alternating factors 1 − (−q)iX. In odd rank the base-change parameter list also contains 1. Its factor (1 − y)−1 cancels the final numerator 1 − qn−1X, as the rank-one base case requires. This accounts for every index 0 ≤ i < n in the uniform product formula. Separation of the first two factors[1145] full product and parity convention[1146]

At the inert place the inverse target character has ε = (−1)b. Thus 1 − (−q)iX = 1 − (−1)b+iq−(2s+n−i). Their product is 1/dv(s). Meanwhile y = ε(q²)−(s+½) uses the norm of the unique extension place. The inverse paired factors, with the extra unit parameter in odd rank, give its twisted L-factor at s + ½. This proves the normalized quotient used in the local factor calculation. For a general arithmetic matrix coefficient the result is multiplied by its value at the identity. Identification of the two products[1147] transport to the arithmetic integral[1148]

7The arithmetic balance

A bound for a centered prime sum can survive a surprisingly large error in a single arithmetic measurement. The proof takes measurements at many places and along a chain, then divides by their total weight. This chapter follows that division and accounts for each power of the scale that it costs.

7.1An identity before an estimate

Write H for the finite abelian group used to label the translations, E = (ℤ/2ℤ)² × H, and Φ for the subgroup whose first coordinate is zero. The character χC equals +1 on Φ and −1 on its complement. The index 0 in a sum over additive characters denotes the character identically equal to one. The map ℓ assigns a complex number to each character. At this stage it is input data. Its identification with logarithmic derivatives belongs to the arithmetic realization. The two halves[1149] The sign character[1150]

Choose a > 0, a translation τ ∈ H, weights wρ > 0 for ρ ∈ Φ, and an integer cutoff N ≥ a/wρ for every such ρ. The host data distinguish a prime d and a finite set S containing 2 and the auxiliary parameter q1, with d outside S. Outside S and d inertia is trivial. At primes of S, both inertia and the specified Frobenius element lie in Φ. At d, the inertia elements are exactly zero and the involution sgc0 = ((1,0),0). Inertia here records the local symmetries invisible on the residue field. Frobenius describes raising residues to the residue-field size. The source packages these assumptions as HostFactsS. Host hypotheses[1151]

Write A for the weighted prime-power count at one sample and one chain stage. To assign a weight to g outside Φ, pair it with ρ = ((1,1),0) + g + ((0,0),τ) inside Φ. At n = pi the weight is (a/n − wρ)+, where the subscript means the positive part. At an unramified prime the character sum is 2 if g equals the ith Frobenius power and zero otherwise. Its contribution is therefore twice log p times the weight when that power lies outside Φ. At a prime of S the Frobenius coset lies inside Φ and contributes zero. At d the inertia subgroup has order two, so averaging replaces 2 by 1 at each matching element outside Φ. Each such weight contributes log d times its value. These three calculations identify the count with the finite character expansion. Local counts and normalization[1152] The three character sums[1153]

For v = wρ the identity (a/n − v)+ = v(a/(v n) − 1)+ changes the scale to y = a/v. Terms beyond the cutoff vanish. Write Gψ(y) for the centered ramp. For a nontrivial ψ it sums the von Mangoldt weight, multiplied by the local character value and y/n − 1, over 1 ≤ n ≤ y, then adds y ℓ(ψ). For the trivial character it uses the centered zeta ramp. Substitution gives the following main term, where γ is Euler’s constant. The centered character ramp[1154] Main term and remainder[1155]

M = a log a − (1 + γ)a − (a/|Φ|) ∑ρ ∈ Φ log wρ + a ℓ(χC).

The trivial character gives the first three terms. For the other characters the centering contributes −a ℓ(ψ). Summing the conjugate phases over the complementary half of E kills the nonconstant characters except χC, whose sum is −|Φ|. This accounts for the plus sign. The pairing of the two halves permutes the weight indices, giving precisely the average of their logarithms. The remainder A − M is the same character average with centered ramps in the summands. This proves the analytic identity at fixed host data. Identifying the degrees, periods, heights and covolumes of the geometric construction with this particular M is an additional theorem. Balance identity and sign calculation[1156] The identification consumed by the geometric estimate[1157]

At one translation the lattice calculation uses the sum over all sampled indices t and stages j. Its total amplitude was denoted by A = ∑t at. Here the object being summed is the count At,j just computed, and its main term is Mt,j. The two identifications together make the geometric residual exactly ∑t,j (At,j − Re Mt,j). This equality is what allows the character average to use the geometric bound. Identification of the aggregate main term[1158] The residual before averaging[1159]

7.2Which characters survive?

Let A0 be a subgroup of H. For ψ a character of E, put Sψ = ∑u ∈ A₀ ψ(0, −u). Translation by any v ∈ A0 permutes this sum and multiplies it by ψ(0, −v). Thus the sum vanishes whenever one of these multipliers differs from one. Otherwise it equals |A0|. For e1(τ) = ((1,0),τ) and s ∈ A0, the corresponding shifted sum acquires the phase ψ(e1(τ)). Summing over s ∈ T2 ⊆ A0 and averaging over subgroup translations therefore contributes a density δ2/2 with δ2 = |T2|/|H|. The two in the denominator comes from |Φ| = 2|H|. Translation and density identities[1160]

For example, take H = ℤ/4ℤ and A0 = {0, 2}. On H the four characters are ψj(h) = exp(2πijh/4) for j = 0, 1, 2, 3. Averaging ψj over A0 gives (1 + (−1)j)/2. The odd indices cancel and the even ones survive with value 1. If T2 contains one element, its contribution occupies one of the eight positions in Φ. The factor 1/8 comes from that count, independently of which surviving character is evaluated.

At a scale x ≥ 3, fix a loss ε > 0, a real sampling weight c with |c| ≤ 1, and a finite sample T ⊆ H. The survivors form the annihilator Ψ of A0. A further selection K ⊆ Ψ retains characters used in the target. For these the source imposes ψ(sgc0) = 1 and includes the trivial character. Among retained characters, a character trivial on all of H receives weight 1. The others receive c. Call these weights ωψ. For retained characters nontrivial on H, the sum over T of ψ(0,τ) differs from c|T| in norm by at most M0x−1+ε|T|, where M0 also bounds |Ψ|. The constants bounding ℓ on retained nontrivial and discarded characters are respectively K0 and CE log x. The sum of norms of the discarded centered ramps is denoted Σ. Orthogonality by itself leaves this last error to be paid. Weights, discarded sum and sampling assumptions[1161]

7.3Dividing the error by the observed weight

Write n = |H|, t = |T|, v = |T2|, m for the length of the chain and b for its positive weight scale. At a translation τ the measurement uses an amplitude aτ with |aτ/b − x| ≤ 1. In the realized chain aE is the size parameter Dd.a, and the adjustable positive parameter k is real. For each subgroup translation, Err bounds the sum, over all t samples and m chain positions, of A − Re M. Weights and translated gaps[1162]

For each subgroup translation u, the local comparison keeps the indices ((0,1),s + u) with s ∈ T2. The source calls these the thick indices. At those indices b ≤ w ≤ b + η + 1 with η ≥ 0. Replacing w by b changes the weighted ramp by at most 3(x + 1)(η + 1). At each other index in Φ, w ≤ 2b′. The parameters satisfy b′, X′ > 0 and b′X′ ≤ xb, so aτ/w ≥ X′/3. On this range assume ‖Gψ(y)‖ ≤ yθ with θ ≥ 0. Omitting that term costs at most (x + 1)bθ. With f = |Φ|, the normalized character sum multiplies the sum of these two allowances by at most 2f. The conditions 6f(x + 1)(η + 1) ≤ b/x and 2f(x + 1)θ ≤ 1/x give a total allowance of 2b/x per measurement. Termwise comparison[1163] The two local cost conditions[1164] Thick indices[1165]

At the central scale define the signed real signal B = ∑ψ ∈ K ωψ Re Gψ(x) − Σ, where Σ = ∑ψ ∈ Ψ ∖ K ‖Gψ(x)‖. Also put Q = t m b. The estimate takes the form

Q (v/2n)(B − 4X) ≤ Err + 2Q/x,   X = x1/2+ε.

For positive observed weight Qv/(2n), direct division shows what an error costs. The upper bound for B is 4X + (2n/v)(Err/Q + 2/x). In the four-translation example v/(2n) = 1/8, so a unit of normalized error Err/Q increases the allowance by eight. A large negative B already satisfies the inequality. Its use later in the proof therefore requires the specific linear combinations of characters that recover the desired upper bound.

For each surviving character, the source bounds the real part of its phase-weighted sample sum from below, comparing each aτ/b with x. After summation the lower bound is t(B − 4X). Averaging the local upper bounds over the subgroup introduces the factor v/(2n). The signed lower and upper estimates then give the displayed inequality. The norms in Σ permit the discarded characters to contribute with either sign. Single-character lower bound[1166] From translated gaps to a scalar inequality[1167] Application of the scalar lemma[1168]

Assume x ≥ 3, ε > 0, C ≥ 0, b > 0, n ≥ 1, 0 ≤ aE ≤ 2x b. The scalar size hypothesis bounds Err by xCε times the sum of four quantities. The right column gives each quotient after division by Q. Complete scalar hypotheses[1169]

ContributionAfter division by t m b
t aEaE/(m b)
t aEm²/kaEm/(b k)
m(2n m b xε)2(n/t)m xε
m v k b xε/(n²x−ε)(v/t)(k/n²)x2ε

The leading scales are consequently x/m, xm/k, m, k/n². Balancing the first and third suggests m near √x. This heuristic by itself supplies neither admissible ranks nor densities. The size lemma actually assumes

x1/2−ε ≤ m ≤ x1/2+ε/2,   xm ≤ k ≤ n²x1/2−ε,
t ≥ ½n x−ε/8,   x−ε ≤ v/n ≤ 1,   x3ε/8 ≥ 26.

These conditions give Q > 0. Set Y = x1/2+13ε/8. The first quotient is at most 2X ≤ 2Y. The second is at most 2 by the lower bound on k. For the third use n/t ≤ 2xε/8 and the upper bound on m to get 4Y. For the fourth, v ≤ n gives v/t ≤ 2xε/8. Its upper bound is 2x1/2+9ε/8 ≤ 2Y. Altogether Err/Q ≤ 10xCεY. This is where the admissible interval for k matters. Both endpoints must hold at the same scale. Four separate bounds[1170]

Since 2/x ≤ 1 and xCεY ≥ 1, the scalar inequality gives (v/n)(B − 4X) ≤ 22xCεY. Divide by the positive density, whose reciprocal is at most xε. Then B ≤ 26x1/2+(C+21/8)ε. The last threshold absorbs 26 and gives the exponent 1/2 + (C + 3)ε. The written proof of ch_core passes the signed B and the averaged inequality directly to proposition_size_bound. Its proof calls the four component bounds in the same file. The scalar size lemma[1171]

7.4What does one arithmetic measurement buy?

Fix a level, a scale x in its arithmetic window and the sampling data at that scale. At translation σ, subtract the predicted main term from the prime-power count and sum over the samples and chain stages. Call this real difference Δσ. The lattice argument gives an upper bound Err for each Δσ. The character calculation reads the same differences in the opposite direction. Write B for the weighted sum of the retained real parts after subtracting the allowance for discarded characters.

Set X = x½+ε and write Q for the total weight. It is the product of the number of samples, the number of stages and the weight per measurement. The average runs over the translation subgroup. At each translation the calculation keeps v of the 2n weight positions, a fraction v/(2n). Replacing their individual weights by a common weight and bounding the omitted terms costs the additive 2Q/x. Upper bound for one translation · The averaged comparison

Q · [v/(2n)](B − 4X) ≤ meanσ Δσ + 2Q/x ≤ Err + 2Q/x.
Which part of this chain can a normalized theta coefficient justify?

In a differentiated theta series, the coefficient of a monomial of degree j in one variable is multiplied by j! when its jth derivative is evaluated at zero. After the section and its coordinates have been normalized, a valuation estimate on that derivative controls divisibility of a lattice-map entry. This contributes to the upper bound on Δσ. The other use of theta, constructing nonzero global lifts, supplies the Galois row used to select a window. There the weighted cohomology lengths fit within √b, with b the weight per measurement. Setting Err equal to √b would drop the other costs of the lattice comparison. The factorial in the entry · How the lifts supply the row · Where the length bound enters

If the total allowance is 60, how far above 4X can B lie?

For an arithmetic check on the division, take Q = 80, v/(2n) = ¼ and Err + 2Q/x = 60. The observed weight is 20, giving B ≤ 4X + 3. A value 100 below 4X also satisfies the inequality. Recovering the fixed family sum requires adding back the allowance for discarded characters. The analytic test then uses the positive part of that family sum. Recovery of the level sum · The positive part in the pole test

Would measurements at both ends of the interval suffice?

A continuous positive bump between the endpoints can have any prescribed integral while vanishing at both ends. The arithmetic construction provides estimates throughout one interval for the same level sum. Passing to u = log x gives the integral bound on that interval, and arbitrarily distant such intervals are available. Carry the bound across the whole interval.

7.5Recovering the level sum

For a level Λ of order o, core_gm applies the preceding argument with c = 1/(3o + 1) and M0 = 4o. The hypotheses EAtH and CoreAtH supply the local character estimates and compatible chain data at the chosen scale. In particular eD + eL ≥ 0 and the error exponent C can be taken as eD + eL + 3. Each discarded character contributes at most x1/2+ε in norm. Counting the entire annihilator bounds Σ by 4o x1/2+ε. Thus GΛ is at most (1 + 4o)x1/2+(eD+eL+6)ε. Choosing x large enough that xε ≥ 1 + 4o gives

GΛ(x) ≤ x1/2+(eD+eL+7)ε.

The exponent applies to scales carrying the required data. A fixed ε allows thresholds depending on the level and constants, uniformly in the later choices of host and sample. The window construction supplies such scales. The level bound[1172] Discarded characters[1173] Transport to family windows[1174]

The third-place construction used by the final theorem chooses eD = 2 and eL = 0. The argument order is visible in topDesWin, which passes those two real numbers on as the family exponents. This specialization gives 1/2 + 9ε. Parameter choice[701] Transport of the exponents[1175]

8Supplying the arithmetic hypotheses

The arithmetic estimate uses many fields and many primes. To control their total contribution, the proof bounds the lengths of cohomology groups on carefully chosen intervals. This is where one must keep track of which parameters have already been fixed when a field or window is chosen.

What length measures · The allowance per measurement · The three contributions · Tower generators · Descent · Selecting the interval · The degree-two bound · Detecting cycles · Counting faces · The plus bound · Trace congruences · The minus bound · The Frobenius test · Choosing both primes · The final window

8.1From Galois representations to window data

Over a CM field E, the row hypothesis applies to a regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representation of positive rank a. A CM field is a totally imaginary quadratic extension of a totally real field. In this setting a polarization relates a representation to a twist of its conjugate dual. For each allowed ℓ-adic coefficient realization, the conclusion gives a representation of the absolute Galois group on an a-dimensional ℓ-adic vector space, a weight and Hodge–Tate weight data. Its package of requirements includes continuity, semisimplicity and prescribed local compatibility. The local theory uses both places above ℓ and places away from ℓ. The window construction uses this row directly and to obtain its open-image input, together with the base-change theorem. Galois row hypotheses and conclusion[1176] Construction from the row[1177]

The separate chapter on the two theta lifts explains the Galois input. For the derivative estimate used on the geometric side, see the factorial gain and the mixed-coordinate correction. The estimate on cohomology below has different indices and quantifiers.

8.2What the good arithmetic window controls

One can first think of a degree-one cohomology class as a way of assigning a value to each symmetry. A cocycle satisfies c(gh) = c(g) + g·c(h). Two choices give the same class if they differ by g ↦ g·a − a. For the group of order two acting trivially on ℤ/4, the choice at its generator must double to zero. The two possibilities 0 and 2 give exactly two classes. In the arithmetic problem the group is a Galois group, the action includes a twist and one retains classes whose restrictions vanish at the specified places. This is the reason a kernel of a restriction map occurs below.

We measure a finite ℤℓ-module by its length. Filter it until each successive quotient has order ℓ. If there are d quotients, its order is ℓd. Both ℤ/ℓ² and (ℤ/ℓ)² have length two, although they require different numbers of generators. Later the tower estimate uses both quantities. Over a coefficient ring with residue field of size ℓf, each quotient instead contributes f to the base-ℓ logarithm of the order.

Fix a number field E and a rational prime ℓ. The coefficient module here is the discrete quotient ℚℓ/ℤℓ. A Tate twist changes the scalar by which Galois acts. If the ℓ-adic cyclotomic character is χcyc, the action on this quotient uses χcyc−j for the integer j in the window sum. With this action the cocycle rule above becomes c(gh) = c(g) + χcyc(g)−jc(h). Vanishing on restriction means the restricted cocycle becomes a coboundary.

The source uses the Galois group with ramification allowed in the specified set of primes above ℓ. The set S in LData is precisely the finite places dividing ℓ. One chooses a place of the algebraic closure above each member and restricts to the corresponding decomposition group. Write hℓ,j for the ℤℓ-module length of the subgroup Sha of these locally trivial degree-one classes. The related degree-two group has coefficients ℤℓ(j + 1). Thus the locally trivial subgroup within degree one is the intersection of the kernels of those local restriction maps. The length bounded by VVle is its ℤℓ-module length. Intersection of restriction kernels[1178] Local data, twists and lengths[1179] Maps to the global Galois group[1180]

Given t and B, VVle demands finiteness of every hℓ,j for 1 ≤ j < t, for all allowed choices of closure and local data. For every finite set P of rational primes it also requires

∑ℓ ∈ P (log ℓ) ∑1 ≤ j < t hℓ,j ≤ B.

The field varies with a primitive character ψ, the height in a cyclotomic tower, and two auxiliary primes q,d. In a cyclotomic field containing the relevant roots of unity, IsChiField specifies the subgroup fixing E by the intersection of four conditions on the exponent of an automorphism: congruence to ±1 modulo 2e+2, ψ(a) = 1, and two quadratic-symbol conditions at q and d. For a fixed ψ and 0 < ε < 1/52, choose any integer function e(x) satisfying x2+8ε ≤ 2e(x) ≤ 2x2+8ε for all x ≥ 1. Then VWin supplies J ≥ 1 and a threshold X0. For every X beyond it and every admissible pair (q,d) at scale X1/J, there is Y ≥ X1/J with Y² ≤ X. Throughout [Y,Y²], every such field satisfies the length bound for t = ⌊x401⌋ and B = exp(xε/2). An admissible pair must obey the prime, congruence, divisibility and logarithmic size conditions of WinPair. Field, auxiliary primes and complete quantifiers[1181]

8.3Splitting the obstruction by the action of conjugation

There is a different estimate for each of three parts of the cohomological sum. To see where they come from, fix a CM field in the construction, a twist index j and an odd prime ℓ. Complex conjugation on the CM field induces a linear involution c on the degree-one cohomology. Its action preserves the locally trivial subgroup. Put s = (−1)j. Because 2 is a unit in ℤℓ, every locally trivial class v has a decomposition

v = ½(v + scv) + ½(v − scv).

Applying c to the first summand multiplies it by s, and applying it to the second multiplies it by −s. Both still lie in the subgroup. A vector in both eigenspaces satisfies 2sv = 0, hence vanishes. The sum is direct, so the full module length equals the sum of its two eigenspace lengths. The name “plus” in the source means eigenvalue (−1)j; for odd j this is the −1 eigenspace. At ℓ = 2 the projectors involve a forbidden division, and the full module is estimated separately. Direct-sum construction[1182] Conjugation and the two parities[1183]

On the joint window there are bounds B2 on the sum of full lengths at ℓ = 2, and B+ and B− on the logarithmically weighted odd-prime sums of the two corresponding lengths. Each comes with finiteness for its twists and primes. Length additivity gives finiteness of the full group at odd primes as well. For any finite prime set, split off 2 if present, and add the two odd-prime inequalities term by term. This proves the bound B2 log 2 + B+ + B−. It explains why the factor log 2 appears only on the first term. Finiteness hypotheses and combination theorem[1184]

8.4Putting the three estimates on one interval

Existence of two arbitrarily distant intervals separately would give no control of their intersection. The source instead constructs a window satisfying a specified condition IsBWindow, which includes a bound at 2 and bounds on certain layers of auxiliary prime towers. The plus estimate is proved on every window satisfying this condition, once the same prime pair is large enough. Choose the maximum of the two thresholds for X, and an upper bound for the finitely many forbidden-size parameters for the two primes. An interval supplied by the first theorem then satisfies the second theorem with the same endpoints, field and tower level. The minus estimate applies to the composite CM field without any further window choice. Definition of the common window[1185] Quantifiers of the plus estimate[1186] Joint window assembly[1187]

Write NE for the conductor of the field, t for the twist cutoff and u = NEt. On the accepted window u ≥ 1 and log u ≤ 2xε/4. Indeed NE ≤ 2e+2Nψqd. Taking logarithms, the page bound and t ≤ x401 contribute at most a fixed constant plus a constant times log x; the pair satisfies log(qd) ≤ xε/4. The first terms are eventually absorbed in a second xε/4. With constants C,K fixed before x, the three bounds take the form

B2 = exp(x4ε/5),   B− ≤ K exp(8xε/4),
B+ = uC + C exp(x4ε/5).

For u ≥ 1, uC ≤ exp(2|C|xε/4). Every exponent on the right of the displayed estimates is o(xε) for fixed ε > 0. Beyond a common threshold each exponential is at most exp(xε/4), and the sum of the fixed nonnegative prefactors, including log 2 and absolute values for constants, is itself at most exp(xε/4). Their product proves the required exp(xε/2). This comparison is uniform over fields obeying the conductor bound. Conductor estimate[1188] Minus contribution[1189] Uniform error ceiling[1190] Assembly for the chosen field[1191]

The tower estimate uses a bound on degree-two cohomology, Poitou–Tate duality, local finiteness, local Tate duality and the Ferrero–Washington theorem. The plus contribution also uses separate representation counts. The following argument explains how the number of generators of a tower module controls the choice of the common interval. Inputs to the tower estimate[1192] Use at twist cutoff exponent 401[1193]

8.5What Ferrero–Washington supplies in this proof

A generator bound limits how many independent ℓ-adic directions can contribute to the growth of a cohomology group. The argument starts with the ideal class groups of the number fields in the finite layers of a cyclotomic tower, passes to a single module for the infinite tower, and then recovers the length at any chosen finite layer as a quotient of that module. The class group of a number field is the group of its nonzero fractional ideals modulo principal ideals.

Write Cl(L) for the ideal class group of a number field L, written additively. The number of independent characters of order ℓ depends on Cl(L)/ℓCl(L). For an abelian extension K/ℚ containing a primitive ℓth root of unity, or a primitive fourth root of unity at ℓ = 2, the statement called Published.FerreroWashington gives a single integer r such that

|Cl(K(μℓⁿ))/ℓCl(K(μℓⁿ))| ≤ ℓr   for every n ≥ 0.

Here μℓⁿ denotes the roots of unity of order dividing ℓn. The constant can depend on ℓ and K. The name Published occurs in the type of the result. The actual window proof passes the theorem FW.ferreroWashington, whose written body constructs r. Class-group statement[1194] Construction of the exponent[1195] Use by the window proof[1193]

First work in the full cyclotomic fields L = ℚ(μfℓⁿ) for fixed f > 1 prime to ℓ. Let C = Cl(L), let J be complex conjugation, and write E = (1 − J)C. The source supplies a bound B0 for the index of ℓC + (1 − γ)C, for its chosen Galois element γ. It also supplies N and n0, independent of n, such that in the integral group ring (γ − 1)N belongs to the ideal generated by θ, 1 + J and ℓ for n ≥ n0. Here θ is the integral element thetaH, whose coefficients use one representative from each pair of opposite residues. Stickelberger annihilation gives θ(1 − J)C = 0. The source selects the smoothing integer 2fℓ + 1. Uniform group-ring relation[1196] Uniform index bound[1197] Stickelberger annihilation[1198] Choice of parameter and cyclotomic cases[1199]

Put T = 1 − γ. Multiply the relation by 1 − J. The θ term kills the class group, the 1 + J term disappears because J² = 1, and the last term has image inside ℓE. Hence TN kills V = E/ℓE. Each quotient TaV/Ta+1V is an image of V/TV. The map 1 − J in turn sends C/(ℓC + TC) onto V/TV. Multiplying the at most N quotient sizes gives |V| ≤ B0N. On the finite group E, the kernel and cokernel of multiplication by ℓ have the same order, so the same bound holds for |E[ℓ]|. Group-ring relation acting on the class group[1200] Bound for a nilpotent endomorphism[1201]

At odd ℓ a reflection inequality bounds |C/(ℓC + E)| by ℓ times the number of ℓ-torsion elements on which conjugation acts by −1. Each such element x lies in E, since (1 − J)(((ℓ + 1)/2)x) = x, with the integer scalar (ℓ + 1)/2. The remaining factor |(ℓC + E)/ℓC| is at most |E/ℓE|. The resulting bound is ℓB02N. At ℓ = 2 put C− = ker(1 + J). The separate sign estimate gives [C−∶E] ≤ (2φ(4f))N, where φ is Euler’s totient. On C[2], the map 1 − J has image in E[2] and kernel in C−[2]. The latter has order at most [C−∶E] |E[2]|. The source uses the looser uniform bound ([C−∶E] |E[2]|)². Reflection at odd primes[1202] Odd-prime index product[1203] Sign estimate at 2[1204] Two-primary index bound[1205]

To transfer either bound, denoted by B, to the abelian field K, use its inclusion in a cyclotomic field. The embedding lemma chooses f,D before n. For every K′ = K(μℓⁿ) it produces a full cyclotomic field L of conductor fℓm, with m ≥ n0 and [L∶K′] ≤ Dℓn₀. Restrict the unramified ℤ/ℓ-characters from K′ to L. The size of the restriction kernel is bounded by the subgroup index [L∶K′], and the Artin character comparison bounds its image by the number of class-group characters of L. Thus |Cl(K′)/ℓCl(K′)| ≤ Dℓn₀B. The written proof chooses this integer itself for r, since it is at most ℓr. The arithmetic inputs to this derivation include the group-ring relation, the uniform ambiguous-class index, Stickelberger annihilation, reflection and the sign estimate at 2. Their statements have the pinned suppliers above. Embedding and degree calculation[1206] Restriction of class-group characters[1207] Uniform transfer[1195]

8.6From class-group characters to generators

Let U∞ be the kernel of the ℓ-adic cyclotomic character on the absolute Galois group, and put A = ℚℓ/ℤℓ. For an integer s ≥ 1, let Ds be the group of locally constant homomorphisms U∞ → A vanishing on its intersections with every inertia group and with each decomposition group above a prime dividing s. Define Xs = Homℤℓ(Ds, A). The earlier cokernel calculation uses s = ℓ. The generator proof starts at s = 1. Local conditions on the characters[1208] Definition of the character module[1209] Its ℤℓ-linear dual[1210]

At the finite field K(μℓⁿ), n ≥ 2, class field theory pulls the class-group characters onto the everywhere unramified ℤ/ℓ-characters. Their number is bounded by the cardinality of Cl/ℓCl, since they factor through that finite vector space and its dual has the same dimension. At infinite level every such character extends to a finite level. The extension theorem first extends the locally constant homomorphism and then enforces the local conditions after moving higher. Compactness of the relevant sets of decomposition and inertia elements makes a single higher level suffice. For the second, apply σ and expand the trace as a sum over τ ∈ G. Linear independence of distinct field automorphisms as functions of x identifies the coefficient of τ(x) on both sides.

b0x = ∑i Tr(xfi)ei,   ∑i τ(fi)σ(ei) = b0 δστ.

Suppose r0(b0) ≠ 0. For a prescribed tuple (vτ), lift each scalar ∑τvτr(τfi)/r0(b0) to a coefficient ci in 𝒪L′ using surjectivity of r0. Then a = ∑iciei has exactly the specified tuple by the second identity. Conversely, if every entry for a vanishes, each integral trace Tr(afi) belongs to ker r0. The first identity shows that b0a belongs to (ker r0)𝒪F. In the quotient b0 has an inverse lifted from k, so a belongs to the same ideal. Its elements all have zero tuple since every σ fixes the base. We have obtained the ring isomorphism

𝒪F / (ker r0)𝒪F ≃ ∏σ∈G k.

The trace formula constructs the required coefficients without choosing an integral basis over the base ring. A linear basis over the field and a common denominator suffice.
