Write Aγ for the linear action of γ on Hermitian matrices. From a smooth function φ on the cone form the weights ψγ(h) = φ(Aγ⁻¹h). Only finitely many terms occur near any point, and they sum to 1. For a cochain β whose values are forms, let K insert a new first argument and average with these weights. Write δ for the alternating deletion of group arguments and d for exterior differentiation. The construction is

(Kβ)(g₀,…) = ∑γ ψγ β(γ,g₀,…),   η₀ = c,   ηj+1 = d(Kηj).

In Kδβ, deleting the newly inserted γ gives β times ∑ψγ = β. Every other deletion cancels the corresponding term of δKβ. Thus δK + Kδ = 1 in the degrees used here. Starting with δη₀ = 0, induction gives δηj+1 = dδKηj = dηj = 0. Indeed η₀ is constant in the cone variable, and every later ηj is an exterior derivative. After m steps only one group argument remains. The equation δηm = 0 now says its values at any two group elements coincide. This leaves a smooth closed form on the cone. Taking B to be a small closed ball about a point of the cone therefore gives the same finite list throughout that ball. The orbit sum S(h) = ∑γ b(τγh) is smooth there. Since τδτγ = τγδ, left multiplication by γ reindexes the sum and makes S invariant. A smooth function on a thickening of the compact set[1500] Relative translates and reindexing the orbit sum[1501] A fixed finite sum on a neighborhood[1502]

Let Θ be the smooth transition from zero on (−∞,0] to one on [1,∞). The denominator g(s) = ½ + (s−½)Θ(2s−1) is at least ½ everywhere and equals s for s ≥ 1. Define ψ = b/g(S) on the cone and extend by zero outside it. Every point outside the cone has a neighborhood disjoint from K′, so the extension is smooth. If γ₀·h lies in K, the term labelled γ₀⁻¹ is at least one in the raw sum. Consequently

∑γ∈Γ ψ(τγh) = S(h)/g(S(h)) = 1   whenever Γ·h meets K.

All elements giving the same orbit point contribute separately to S. Their multiplicity is the order of the stabilizer. The denominator and its two thresholds[1503] Global smoothness, support and uniform bounds[1504] The inverse group element providing a summand of size one[1492]

Two points of one orbit receive different weights

Take 𝒪 = ℤ[ω] with ω² + ω + 1 = 0. Put h₀ = Id₂, s = [[1,1],[0,1]] and h₁ = s∗s = [[1,1],[1,2]]. Every τγh₀ = γ∗γ has entries in 𝒪. Distinct such matrices differ by at least one in the maximum absolute entry norm, because every nonzero Eisenstein integer has absolute value at least one. Choose two disjoint bumps around h₀ and h₁ inside the cone whose supports meet this orbit only at their respective centers. Give their sum b values 1 and 2 at the centers.

The squared length of a column is the sum of two nonnegative integer norms. A unit column therefore has a single nonzero coordinate, one of the six units. Orthogonality puts the second column on the other axis. The stabilizer U of h₀ has 2·6² = 72 elements. Also γ∗γ = s∗s exactly when γs⁻¹ ∈ U, so the labels giving h₁ form U s. At h₀ there are 144 nonzero terms and S = 72·1 + 72·2 = 216. Each label in U receives 1/216 and each label in U s receives 1/108. The two centers receive total weights ⅓ and ⅔.

Pull back the compactly supported weight. Let F be the smooth equivariant map obtained by normalizing the scale and correcting the two minima. Set φ(h) = ψ(F(h)). Every F(h) meets K up to a translate. Hence ∑γ φ(τγh) = 1 for every positive h. For a compact neighborhood V in the input cone, apply properness to F(V) ∪ K′ to get a finite list on its interior. There is also one finite set of relative labels for the whole cone. Let D be the closure in that cone of {φ ≠ 0}. Continuity gives F(D) ⊆ K′. If the supports with labels γ and η meet, some h has γ⁻¹·h and η⁻¹·h in D. Their images under F are in K′ and differ by the action of η⁻¹γ. This puts η⁻¹γ in the single finite set Γ(K′). Choosing the compact set and the uniform constants[1458] Equivariance and smoothness of the corrected map[1505] Pullback, local finiteness and normalization[1506] Overlap of the closed supports in the positive cone[1507]

Why this bump also works for the derivative estimate

Say k is δ-close to positive h if |qk(z)−qh(z)| ≤ δqh(z) for all archimedean columns. Polarization on coordinate vectors gives ‖k−h‖ ≤ 2δ‖h‖ in the matrix-entry norm. The smooth compactly supported ψ has an ordinary Lipschitz constant Lψ. Choose R ≥ 0 bounding the norm on K′. If the two values differ, at least one point belongs to K′. For 0 ≤ δ < ¼ the norm estimate then gives ‖h‖ ≤ 2R, so |ψ(k)−ψ(h)| ≤ 4LψRδ. For δ ≥ ¼ the bound 0 ≤ ψ ≤ 2/m supplies the upper bound 16δ/m. Thus Cψ = 16/m + 4LψR works for every δ ≥ 0, including cases where k lies outside the cone. Composing with the relative bounds for the normalization and correction, then differentiating in a moving frame, gives the one-power height bound. The companion finite-overlap assertion controls the labels present in sums of derivatives. Relative quadratic control in matrix-entry norm[1508] A Lipschitz constant for the compactly supported smooth bump[1509] Large and small relative perturbations[1510] Combining the three relative bounds[1511] Conversion to one power of height[1512] From relative perturbations to a moving-frame derivative[1513] Assembly of the proper action and smooth bump[1514]

Why the exponent is one. Write H(h) = 1/(λ(h)λ∨(h)). Common rescaling preserves H. A perturbation of relative size δ changes every quadratic value by at most δ times that value. The normalization h ↦ h₀ increases this relative error by at most a factor 3 for δ ≤ ¼. For the averaged outer product at scale s, the change is bounded by a constant times δqh₀(z)/s in each test direction z. The active scales for two nearby inputs lie above 3λ(h₀)/64. Summing their reciprocals as a geometric progression costs at most 256/[9λ(h₀)]. To measure this error relative to the output, use qF(h) ≥ μ(h₀)qh₀ and μ ≥ λ∨/4. The reciprocal product of the two minima is exactly H. Including the variations of μ and of the cutoffs gives a total relative error ≤ C(1+H)δ for sufficiently small δ. The bump is Lipschitz for this relative error. Passing to derivatives in the moving frame costs a further factor N, and the positive lower bound H ≥ c₀ gives 1+H ≤ (1+1/c₀)H. The multiplicative constants may depend on L and N. The exponent a = 1 works in every rank N ≥ 1. Geometric sum and the reciprocal product[1515] The interval of active scales[1516] Moving-frame differentiation[1517] The exponent and its prefactor[1518]

For L = ℚ(i) and N = 1, write h = [t], t > 0. Then qh(z) = t|z|² on ℤ[i], λ = t, λ∨ = 1/t, and H = 1. The determinant product is t², so normalization sends every t to 1. All four units ±1, ±i fix every Hermitian scalar. Their four translated partition values are therefore equal, and the orbit sum forces each value to be ¼. Counting only distinct points of this orbit would lose the stabilizer factor. Common-scale normalization[1519] Sum over the arithmetic group[1520]

How the correction keeps both lattice minima positive

The compactness argument needs a constant c > 0 that works for both minima at every input h. Adding positive forms helps its primal minimum but can make its inverse smaller. Why does the dual minimum survive? The proof tests the correction in a direction chosen by an integral covector. Along this direction a whole range of scales vanishes exactly. Where the two bounds enter the partition[1521]

Fix the field L and rank N ≥ 1. Write qh for squared length summed over the infinite places, and λ and λ∨ for the minima on nonzero integral vectors of h and its dual h∨, whose matrix at each place is the inverse transpose. Let R be the corrected form. Its base term is μh, where μ is a smooth approximation to λ∨(h). At scale d = 4j, a lattice vector v contributes a rank-one form with local matrix (hwvw)(hwvw)*. Give it weight θ(qh(v)/d), where 0 ≤ θ ≤ 1, θ = 1 on arguments ≤ 1 and θ = 0 on arguments ≥ 4. Divide the weighted sum by d²Zd, where Zd is the sum of the weights, to obtain Td. The zero vector has weight 1, so this denominator is positive. Then R = μh + ∑d θ(dμ)Td. Two cutoffs and the normalization at one scale[1493]

The primal minimum. Let u attain λ(R) and set a = qh(u). If μa ≥ 1/16, the base term suffices. Otherwise choose a power of four with 4a ≤ d ≤ 16a. Its outer weight is 1. For every v with qh(v) ≤ d/4, both v and v+u have inner weight 1, by the parallelogram identity. Put B = Re ∑w uw*hwvw. Translation by u changes B to B+a, and B²+(B+a)² ≥ a²/2. By Cauchy–Schwarz, each square is at most the number r of infinite places times the corresponding rank-one value at u.

Let M count the vectors in the inner ball of squared radius d/4. The positive weighted numerator at u is at least Ma²/(4r). Indeed, each of the two lists v and v+u has no repetitions, so together they can charge the numerator at most twice. The counting estimate with dilation 16 gives Zd ≤ #{v ∣ qh(v) ≤ 4d} ≤ C₁₆M. Since d ≤ 16a, this one scale proves

λ(R) ≥ min{1/16, 1/(1024rC₁₆)}.

This bound depends on the field and rank through the lattice count. Pairing a lattice vector with its translate[1522] Summing the two lists[1523] Selecting the active scale[1524]

Finding a dual test direction. Now assume L is totally complex. Choose an integral covector f realizing Q = λ∨(R). Among vectors with f(v) ≠ 0, choose v₀ minimizing m = qh(v₀). Such a vector exists because f is nonzero on at least one coordinate vector, and only finitely many lattice vectors have squared length at most that of this first candidate. At some place w we have |f(v₀)w| ≥ 1, because the absolute field norm of this nonzero algebraic integer is at least 1. At that place take the unique y satisfying y*hwx = fw(x) for all x. Set b = y*hwy > 0. The source’s local pairing inequality gives 1 ≤ 4bm. The local inequality, bilinear pairing and integral norm[1525] Choice of covector, vector and place[1526]

The transference bound supplies a lattice point within squared distance ρ = CT/λ∨(h) of any real vector. Apply it at the vector z supported only at w, with component ty where t²b = 5ρ. If the nearby v belonged to the kernel of f, testing z−v against y would give (tb)² ≤ 4bρ. Its left side equals 5bρ. Hence f(v) ≠ 0. The parallelogram identity gives qh(v) ≤ 2(5ρ)+2ρ, so

1 ≤ 4bm,   m ≤ 12CT/λ∨(h).

What the correction does to this direction. When 4d ≤ m, a vector with positive inner weight has qh(v) < m. It lies in the kernel of f by minimality. Thus its rank-one form at w evaluates to |y*hwvw|² = 0. Choose d₀ = 4j₀ ≤ m < 4d₀. Only scales d ≥ d₀ need be counted. For the surviving terms use Cauchy–Schwarz in the original metric. A vector of positive weight has qh(v) < 4d, hence |y*hwvw|² ≤ 4bd. The weighted average divided by d² is at most 4b/d. Their sum is ≤ 4b · (2/d₀) ≤ 32b/m by a geometric series. If μ ≤ Cμλ∨(h), the base term contributes at most 12CT|Cμ|b/m. Put A = 12CT|Cμ|+32. Testing the same covector and vector in the corrected metric now gives

b² = |fw(y)|² ≤ 4Q (y*Rwy) ≤ 4QA b/m,   λ∨(R) = Q ≥ bm/(4A) ≥ 1/(16A).

The selected smoothing permits Cμ = 4. For each fixed field and rank the smaller of the primal and dual bounds works for all positive forms, including the normalized inputs to the partition. Transference away from the kernel[1527] Vanishing below the first active scale and its tail[1528] The dual minimum after the correction[1529] The smoothing comparison[1530]

One scale can raise one direction and leave another untouched. Take ℤ[i]², h = diag(1,64), u = e₁, and use f(v) = v₂ as a test covector. Then m = 64, y = e₂/64 and b = 1/64. At d = 4 the outer weight is 1 since μ ≤ 4λ∨(h) = 1/16. Every vector with positive inner weight is (z,0) with |z|² < 16. There are 45 such Gaussian integer candidates, so Z₄ ≤ 45. The four points at each squared norm 1, 2 and 4 carry full weight. They contribute 4(1+2+4) = 28 to the numerator at e₁. Hence T₄[e₁] ≥ 28/(16·45) = 7/180, while T₄[y] = 0 exactly. This checks the two estimates on one scale without needing the value of the smooth cutoff between its plateaus.

How does a dual minimum put a lattice point near every target?

The dual test needs a lattice point near a prescribed vector that can have arbitrary real coordinates. A lower bound on the length of every nonzero integral covector supplies a covering radius for the original lattice. We derive the bound first in integer coordinates, then identify which dual lattice appears in the arithmetic statement. All costs below are squared distances. The two transference statements[1531] The covering radius used in the dual test[1532]

Find one short direction. For a positive definite real symmetric matrix G of size d ≥ 1 write QG(x) = xᵀGx. Suppose QG⁻¹(c) ≥ δ > 0 for all nonzero integer columns c. To control QG, factor G = BᵀB. The inverse image under B of the box with |yⱼ| ≤ 2|det B|1/d has volume 4d. It is symmetric and convex and its volume exceeds 2d, the Minkowski threshold for ℤd. It therefore contains a nonzero integer v. Summing the coordinate squares of Bv gives QG(v) ≤ 4d(det G)1/d. In particular a positive lower bound ℓ on every nonzero integer vector forces ℓd ≤ (4d)d det G. The volume of the pulled-back box[1533] Its nonzero integer point[1534] From the box to the determinant[1535]

Apply that determinant inequality to G⁻¹ with ℓ = δ and to G under the supposition that all its nonzero integer vectors have squared length greater than 2(4d)²/δ. Multiplication cancels the two determinants and gives 2d ≤ 1. Consequently there is a nonzero integer vector with QG(v) ≤ 2(4d)²/δ. Write this vector as an integer multiple of a primitive one, whose coordinates have greatest common divisor one. The primitive vector is at least as short and can be completed to an integral basis by Smith normal form. In that basis the first diagonal entry of the Gram matrix is its squared length, say a. An integral basis change permutes the lattice vectors and its inverse transpose permutes integral covectors, so both the dual lower bound and the covering problem survive. Scaling the determinant inequality[1536] Applying the estimate to both matrices[1537] Completing the primitive direction[1538] Changing the integral basis[1539]

Round one coordinate after the others. Write the new matrix in blocks [[a,bᵀ],[b,D]] and put S = D − bbᵀ/a. For an error vector (u,y), completing the square gives

QG(u,y) = a(u + bᵀy/a)² + QS(y).

Minimizing in u shows that S is positive definite. For an integral covector c′ on the remaining coordinates, solving Gx = (0,c′) gives x′ = S⁻¹c′. Hence QS⁻¹(c′) = QG⁻¹(0,c′), and the same δ works in dimension d−1. For a target (p₀,p′), use induction to choose an integer c′ with small remaining error y = p′−c′. Round p₀ + bᵀy/a to its nearest integer for the first coordinate. The square on the right now costs at most a/4. Starting with C₀ = 1, the resulting constant satisfies

Cd = Cd−1 + 8d² = 1 + 8 ∑j=1d j²,   QG(p−c) ≤ Cd/δ.

The added cost is at most 2(4d)²/(4δ) by the short-direction bound. In dimension zero the only error is zero, so the initial constant 1 works. The completed square[1540] The dual bound on the smaller form[1541] Rounding with the shift[1542] The initial constant and the induction[1543] Removing the integer multiple and adding the cost[1544] The integer theorem on any finite coordinate set[1545]

Transfer from integral coordinates to Hermitian forms. Let L be totally complex with discriminant Δ, and take a positive definite Hermitian form h at each complex place in rank N ≥ 1. Choose an integral basis b₁,…,be of 𝒪L, where e = [L:ℚ]. The archimedean quadratic form qh acquires a real Gram matrix G in d = Ne coordinates. Every target tuple has real coordinates in this basis, and integer coordinates give the original arithmetic lattice. The integer theorem requires a lower bound for the inverse real Gram matrix. The input λ∨(h) measures integral covectors using (hw⁻¹)ᵀ at each place w.

For a nonzero integer covector c, let T have entries Tr(bᵢbⱼ), hence det T = Δ. In each block multiply the row of coefficients of c by the adjugate of T, then use those integers as basis coefficients of f ∈ 𝒪LN. Since adj(T)T = ΔI, this gives Tr(fₖbⱼ) = Δckj and f ≠ 0. If z is the tuple represented by real coordinates x, linearity and conjugate pairing of the embeddings give Δcᵀx = 2 Re ∑w fwᵀzw. The factor 2 counts the two embeddings at each complex place. The doubled real part in the trace[1546] The trace matrix and its adjugate[1547] Real coordinates at all the complex places[1548]

Now choose x representing zw = hw⁻¹ fw. Set s = qh∨(f). Then QG(x) = s and Δcᵀx = 2s. Expanding the nonnegative square QG(tx−G⁻¹c) gives QG⁻¹(c) ≥ 2t cᵀx−t²s. Substitute t = 2/Δ. Every integral c ≠ 0 now satisfies QG⁻¹(c) ≥ 4s/Δ² ≥ 4λ∨(h)/Δ². Applying the integer result with this δ gives, for each target z, a lattice point v satisfying

qh(z−v) ≤ CdΔ²/(4λ∨(h)).

Thus the constant CT in the dual probe bound depends on the field and rank, and the dependence on the input form is carried by its dual minimum. The short spanning argument uses the same covering estimate. The Hermitian dual and the completed square[1549] The discriminant in the covering constant[1550] Constructing the test vector and returning to the arithmetic lattice[1551] Supplying transference to the partition[1514] The nearby-point argument for thick representatives[1552]

Check the rounding shift and the discriminant on a Gaussian lattice

Take L = ℚ(i), N = 1, h = 1 and the integral basis (1,1+i). Its Gram matrix is [[1,1],[1,2]]. Coordinates (2/5,2/5) give the complex target 4/5 + 2i/5. Rounding both coordinates separately gives the lattice point 0 and squared error 4/5. The Schur complement equals 1. After rounding the second coordinate to 0, the shifted first coordinate is 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/5. Rounding it to 1 gives squared error (−1/5)² + (2/5)² = 1/5.

In this basis the trace matrix is [[2,2],[2,0]], with determinant −4. The integer covector (0,1) times its adjugate is (−2,2), giving f = −2 + 2(1+i) = 2i. Since |f|² = 4, the converted lower bound for this covector is 4·4/(−4)² = 1. Direct multiplication by G⁻¹ = [[2,−1],[−1,1]] gives the same value. This example uses the squared length convention in both calculations.

Which central directions still need averaging?

The form ω realizing the cocycle already has two symmetries. It is invariant under Γ = GLN(𝒪L′) and under a common positive scaling at all infinite places. The next estimate uses independent scalar changes at every place. Write c(t) for the central matrix whose component at w is exp(tw)I. A complex scalar zw acts on a positive Hermitian matrix by Hw ↦ |zw|−2Hw, since the action uses the inverse matrix on the right and its adjoint on the left. Thus only the real logarithms tw = log |zw| matter. The initial symmetries[1553] The action of a scalar[1554]

Let r be the number of complex places of the totally complex field L′. The line of constant vectors in ℝr acts trivially on ω by pullback. A unit u gives another symmetry because uI ∈ Γ. Its logarithm vector ℓ(u) = (log |w(u)|)w lies in V = {t ∈ ℝr ∣ ∑w tw = 0} by the product formula. Dirichlet’s unit theorem gives a lattice Λ of rank r − 1 in V, generated by the logarithms of fundamental units. Subtracting the coordinate mean from any t leaves a vector in V. Consequently the central parameters still to be averaged form the compact torus V/Λ. For r = 1 the initial symmetries already suffice. The logarithms of fundamental units[1555] Removing the constant direction[1556]

The proof integrates one unit direction v = ℓ(u) at a time. For the pullback of the form, including its tangent arguments, it takes

Avω = ∫₀¹ c(τv)∗ω dτ.

Unit invariance makes the integrand 1-periodic in τ. Translating the interval of integration therefore preserves the average, so every real multiple of v fixes Avω. Central scalars commute, which preserves the directions already treated. Iterating uses ordinary Lebesgue measure of mass one on each unit interval. In the coordinates of the fundamental units their product induces Haar probability on V/Λ. The output ω′ is invariant under every scalar tuple. The pullback and its integral[1557] Translation of one full period[1558] Iteration and all central scalars[1559]

Why does the average have exactly the original periods? Fix a finite bar cycle z based at the identity matrix I. For fixed τ, centrality moves the basepoint of every simplex from I to c(τv)·I, keeping the same group labels. Join the old and new vertices by the simplices of a prism. Its side faces cancel on the cycle because ∂z = 0. The remaining two evaluations agree because ω integrates to a cocycle on simplices. Thus for every τ the sum over the cycle already equals its original value. Interchanging the finite sum, simplex integrals and the unit-interval integral preserves that value. The averaged form still integrates to a cocycle by the same interchange on a boundary. Its moving-frame bound retains the exponent am for a form of degree m, since the path τ ↦ c(τv) is compact and right translation there changes the height by a bounded factor. The basepoint prism[1560] Closure and equality on cycles[1561] The height bound on the compact path[1562]

Check the factor of two and a period

In L′ = ℚ(i,√2), label the two complex places by the sign of √2. For u = 1 + √2 and a = log(1 + √2), the absolute values of u at these places are exp(a) and exp(−a). Take N = 1 and work with the cyclic subgroup generated by u. On the pair of positive numbers (H₁,H₂) set s = (log H₂ − log H₁)/(4a). Under c(τℓ(u)) log H₁ decreases by 2aτ and log H₂ increases by 2aτ, so s goes to s + τ. Averaging (2 + cos(2πs)) ds gives 2 ds. The cycle [u] moves s from 0 to 1 at the identity basepoint. The two primitives 2s + sin(2πs)/(2π) and 2s both increase by 2 along that cycle. On an open arc from 0 to 1/4 their increments differ by 1/(2π).

How large must the matrix be to integrate the coefficients?

Even a finite-volume quotient can have an unbounded function whose square has infinite integral. Here the possible growth occurs at the cusps, where a lattice or its dual has a short vector. For the tuple of Hermitian forms h = x·I, let λ(h) be the infimum of the sum of its values over the complex places on a nonzero integral vector. The height is 1/[λ(h)λ(h∨)], where h∨ = (h⁻¹)T at each place. For every totally complex number field L′ and every integer A ≥ 0, the proof chooses a finite-volume Haar fundamental domain for SLN(𝒪L′) in ∏wSLN(ℂ) on which heightA is integrable whenever N ≥ A + 2. The two lattice minima[1563] Order of the quantifiers[1564] The explicit matrix size[1565]

For a form of degree m, the bound on the norm of its coefficients in the moving frame is K heightam. The partition of unity supplies a for the field before the matrix size is chosen. Squaring calls for A = 2am. The comparison therefore chooses N large enough for this moment, for the separate Hecke stability threshold, for the requested starting size, and for N ≥ 3. This one size works for every cocycle of the specified degree m < r₂(L′). The zeroth moment gives finite volume, so the inequality u ≤ u² + 1 for the coefficient norm also gives integrability of the coefficients themselves. Their mean is now defined. Finite volume and the moment on the same domain[1566] Choosing the size and taking the mean[1448]

Why do finitely many regions suffice for the cusp integral?

Let L be totally complex and set Γ = SLN(𝒪L). In the product of SLN(ℂ) over the complex places, a single matrix can travel arbitrarily far out a cusp. What becomes finite is the choice of arithmetic coordinate system. For fixed L and N ≥ 1, there are finitely many matrices cj and one region S such that for every x, some γ ∈ Γ and some j satisfy cj−1γx ∈ S. Inside S the diagonal parameters can still grow. This is the cover used in the height moment. The cover with its quantifiers[1567] Its use in the moment theorem[1568]

How does a shortest row control the cusp diagonal?

Take a number field L of degree d over ℚ and an adelic invertible matrix g of size N ≥ 1. For a nonzero row x over L, form xg at every place. Its height Hg(x) is the product of the Euclidean lengths at the infinite places, squared at complex places, and the maximum entry norms at the finite places. The product formula makes this height invariant under scaling x by L×. Below any fixed height there are only finitely many rational lines. Place a minimizing row last in a rational basis and factor the resulting matrix as an upper triangular matrix times a maximal compact element. The right compact factor preserves all the row lengths. Reduce the upper left block by induction, keeping the last row in place. Height on rational lines[1569] Existence of the minimum[1570] Choosing the last row[1571]

For N ≥ 2 the only new adjacent pair is the bottom block [[α, u], [0, β]]. Write A = |α|𝔸, B = |β|𝔸 for the products of their normalized local absolute values. The last row has height B. Two-dimensional approximation produces a nonzero rational row whose image under this block has height at most C√(AB), with C depending only on L. Putting the two coordinates in the last two slots gives a competitor for the minimum, since the triangular matrix has zeros to their left. Hence

B ≤ C√(AB)  ⟹  B ≤ C²A.

Induction gives this inequality for every pair of consecutive diagonal entries, with the same constant. Embedding the two-coordinate row[1572] Minimality and the uniform ratio[1573]

Where the square root comes from

If A ≥ B, the row (0, 1) already works. Otherwise put s = (A/B)1/(2d). Divide the block by β. After multiplying its first row by a scalar in L×, the upper left entry is a positive idèle of archimedean size s² times an element of a fixed compact set. Call the adjusted upper right entry a. In an integral basis, (H + 1)d candidate multiples of a fall into Hd boxes after rational translation to clear finite denominators and reduction modulo the integer lattice at infinity. Two lie in one box. Their difference gives a nonzero integer ℓ of L of archimedean size O(H + 1) and c ∈ L such that ℓa + c is integral at all finite places and O(1/H) at infinity. For H = ⌈1/s⌉ both coordinates of the resulting row have size O(s) at infinity. Its finite norm product is bounded by compactness. Restoring β bounds the height by a field constant times B sd = √(AB). Counting the boxes[1574] The scale and the rational row[1575] Multiplying the local bounds[1576]

To obtain the real cusp parameters, take rᵢ = |bᵢᵢ|𝔸1/d. The idèle with value rᵢ at every infinite place and 1 at every finite place has norm rᵢd. Dividing it out leaves a norm-one idèle. Rational diagonal scalings bring these remainders into compact representatives of the norm-one idèle classes. Rational upper triangular row additions bring the entries of the upper unitriangular factor into compact additive representatives. The resulting factorization has the fixed compact triangular set, positive diagonal and maximal compact subgroup used in the cusp cover, with t ri+1 ≤ rᵢ for t = C−2/d. At finite places the positive diagonal is the identity, so for g = (x, 1) the rational change of basis has finite component in a fixed compact set. The three factors[1577] The degree root[1578] The orientation of the inequality[1579]

Check the complex-place exponent over ℚ(i)

Take g∞ = [[1, 2], [0, 3]] and identity at every finite place. Every rational line has a primitive Gaussian integer representative (u, v), whose finite height factors are 1. Its height is |u|² + |2u + 3v|². Height 1 would require a unit u with 3 dividing 2u, since u = 0 gives height 9 for a primitive row. The row (1, −1) attains height 2. Use it as the last row of γ = [[0, −1], [1, −1]]. Multiplying γg∞ on the right by the unitary matrix [[1, 1], [1, −1]]/√2 gives [[−3/√2, 3/√2], [0, √2]]. At finite places γ is integral and invertible, so the triangular factor there can be the identity. The last diagonal idèle has norm 2, and its real parameter is √2. The first has norm 9/2 and real parameter 3/√2.

First choose finitely many rational matrices. Append the identity at the finite places to an archimedean point x. The shortest-row construction supplies a rational matrix η such that ηx has a bounded upper triangular factor, a positive diagonal and a compact factor. The positive diagonal equals the identity at the finite places. Thus the finite part of η belongs to one compact set C, the finite projection of the product of the compact triangular set and the maximal compact subgroup. The subgroup U of matrices integral and invertible at every finite place is open. Its left cosets cover C, and finitely many suffice. In each of these cosets that occurs for a rational η, choose one rational representative a. Then a−1η and its inverse are integral at every finite place. Each entry therefore lies in 𝒪L. Writing δ = a−1η, we have δ ∈ GLN(𝒪L) and δx equals a−1 times the reduced factors. The finite list for this GL cover consists of the inverses g = a−1. Correct the determinant. The unit det δ can be written vNu₀. Here v is a unit and u₀ comes from a finite list. Indeed, express a unit as a root of unity times powers of the fundamental units and reduce each exponent modulo N. The list has at most |μ(L)|Nrank 𝒪L× entries. Put D(u) = diag(u,1,…,1). This gives an integral change of coordinates of determinant one.

γ = v−1D(u₀−1)δ,   det γ = v−Nu₀−1 det δ = 1.

The chart now depends only on (g, u₀). Set G = D(u₀−1)g. At each complex place w choose a scalar zw with zwN det w(G) = 1 and take cj,w = zww(G). This is the precise rationality used for the height bound. The underlying matrix G is defined over L, while the scalar can depend on the place. A determinant correction over the Gaussian integers

Test the correction with N = 2, L = ℚ(i), x = g = I and δ = [[i,1],[0,1]]. Here v = 1 and u₀ = i work. Then γ = [[1,−i],[0,1]]. Choose z = exp(πi/4), so z² = i and c = z diag(−i,1) has determinant one. In this chart c−1γ = z−1δ = [[1,1],[0,1]] diag(i/z,1/z). The last factor is unitary of determinant one. This tests the correction on one admissible triangular factorization. The full list of charts may contain other representatives.

How are the chart bounds shared across places?

Before the determinant correction, write the positive diagonal entries as rᵢ, with t ri+1 ≤ rᵢ for fixed t > 0. Compactness bounds the entries of each triangular factor Bw by M and bounds its diagonal moduli below by M−1. After the correction the local scalar is αw = w(v−1)/zw. Use the same diagonal coordinates at every place by setting

sᵢ = log rᵢ + meanw(log |αw| + log |Bw,ii|).

The local determinant-one equations give ∑isᵢ = 0. Subtracting two places’ determinant equations also gives |log |αw| − log |αw′|| ≤ 2 log M. After removing exp(sᵢ) and moving the diagonal phases into the unitary factor, every triangular entry has modulus at most M⁴ and each diagonal modulus is at least M−4. In each diagonal position their product over the places is one, by the definition of the mean. The common region uses si+1 ≤ sᵢ + 4 log M − log t. These bounds hold across all charts for this field and matrix size. Bounding the triangular factor and its inverse[1587] Comparing two places[1588] The mean and the simple-root bound[1589] The factorization and uniform entry bounds[1590]

Integrate over the cover. Write F for a Haar fundamental domain, and let f be a nonnegative Γ-invariant integrand. Moving pieces of F by Γ gives an upper bound by the integral over the union of the charts. Subadditivity and left invariance of Haar measure then give

∫F f dμ ≤ ∑j ∫S f(cjy) dμ(y).

Overlaps are allowed. Each chart has its own finite height constant, and there are only finitely many summands. For f = heightA the remaining integral on each chart is finite when N ≥ A + 2. This last convergence comes from the decay in the unbounded diagonal variables. Why the cusp integral converges

Reduction theory covers the quotient by finitely many charts. After a fixed translate, each point has a bounded triangular factor, a diagonal factor with entries exp(sᵢ) shared across the complex places, and a unitary factor. The determinant gives ∑sᵢ = 0, and the adjacent entries satisfy si+1 ≤ sᵢ + T for a fixed T. Clearing denominators in a chart gives lower bounds proportional to exp(−2 max sᵢ) and exp(2 min sᵢ) for the primal and dual minima. Set W = ∑i<N|sᵢ − si+1|, using indices 1,…,N. Then max sᵢ − min sᵢ ≤ W, so heightA ≤ C exp(2AW). The chart and its translating matrix[1595] Clearing denominators for both minima[1596] The bound on height[1597]

Write Φ = ∑i<j(sᵢ − sⱼ). A unit box in the logarithms has Haar measure at most C′ exp(−2Φ) for every admissible s in it. Indeed, the packing argument fits at least exp(2Φ) translates of the box in a translate of a fixed compact set, with uniformly bounded overlap. When the coordinates decrease, the gap sⱼ − sj+1 occurs j(N − j) times in Φ, at least N − 1 times. For the allowed upward errors of size T, the cone estimate gives the following quantitative version. Logarithmic boxes and the two sums[1598] The packing estimate[1599] The cone inequality with errors[1600]

2AW − 2Φ ≤ C″ − δ ∑i|sᵢ|,   δ = 2(N − 1 − A)/N > 0.

Index the boxes by the integer parts of their coordinates. The integral over a box with index u is bounded by a constant times exp(−δ ∑|uᵢ|). Summing over all boxes gives a product of convergent geometric series. For instance, along (3t, −t, −t, −t) with t ≥ 0, W = 4t and Φ = 12t. At A = 2 the combined exponential is exp(−8t). At A = 3 it equals 1 along the ray. This explains the strict inequality A < N − 1 in the estimate and leaves the endpoint moment undecided. The moment over one box[1601] Summing all boxes[1602]

How a finite incidence count bounds an angle

Let π be the prime element used in the Hecke average, 𝒪 the ring of integers of the field, and k = 𝒪/(π), of order q ≥ 25. Take N ≥ 3. In SLN(L′) consider three conjugates of SLN(𝒪). The group Kᵣ is Dᵣ−1SLN(𝒪)Dᵣ, where the diagonal matrix Dᵣ has π in its first r positions and 1 elsewhere, for r = 0,1,2. Put Eᵢⱼ = Kᵢ ∩ Kⱼ and B = K₀ ∩ K₁ ∩ K₂. At each vertex Kᵣ, the two incident subgroups stabilize a pair of nested subspaces after reduction modulo π. Such a pair is a flag. The three groups[1603] Reading subspace conditions from scaled entries[1604]

Use coordinates 0,…,N − 1 after conjugating by Dᵣ. The following pairs are in the order used by the angle bound. The first subgroup in each pair is called E and the second E′.

  • In K₀, E₀₁ fixes the line spanned by e₀ and E₀₂ fixes the plane spanned by e₀,e₁.
  • In K₁, E₁₂ fixes the line spanned by e₁ and E₀₁ fixes the hyperplane x₀ = 0.
  • In K₂, E₁₂ fixes the hyperplane x₁ = 0 and E₀₂ fixes its subspace x₀ = x₁ = 0.

Here “fixes” means preserves the subspace as a set. The bipartite graph has a vertex for each subspace of the first or second type, and one edge for each incident pair. Equivalently, take the translates of the two coordinate subspaces under Kᵣ. The stabilizer of their common edge is B. In the first two cases a matrix outside E moves the distinguished line to a different line. Row additions preserving the first line can take that new line to a fixed second coordinate line. Thus all such matrices form one double coset of E. Transposing gives the same result for the distinguished hyperplane in the third case. The first column condition[1605] The second vertex[1606] The hyperplane condition[1607] Moving the line by lifted row operations[1608] The double coset[1609] The transpose argument[1610]

Count the flag choices in a finite group

At any one vertex, the proof passes to the finite group G = Kᵣ/core(B), where core(B) is the intersection of all Kᵣ-conjugates of B. Use the same letters for subgroup images. A real function f constant on the cosets Ek has a value at each vertex of the first type. Suppose its mean is zero. Use the uniform measure on G and form its correlation c(s) = meank f(sk)f(k). It equals ‖f‖² on E. Elsewhere it is constant because it depends only on the double coset. Its mean over s is zero, so its value outside E is nonpositive. The actual finite quotient[1611] The two correlation values[1612]

Average f over left multiplication by E′, writing P′f for the result. Expanding its squared norm and reindexing gives the mean of c(s) over s ∈ E′. Only the elements of E′ ∩ E = B can give a positive contribution. Their proportion is 1/[E′:B]. For a function g constant on the cosets E′k, averaging preserves the pairing with g. Cauchy–Schwarz gives

|⟨f,g⟩| = |⟨P′f,g⟩| ≤ ‖f‖‖g‖ / √[E′:B].

At vertex 0, the matrices I + t e₁₀ in E₀₂ move the line to span(e₀ + t e₁) inside the same plane. Distinct t modulo π give distinct flags, so [E₀₂:B] ≥ q. Likewise I + t e₂₁ in E₀₁ sends e₁ to e₁ + t e₂ while fixing e₀. This supplies [E₀₁:B] ≥ q, the other needed index. Thus every pairing has coefficient at most 1/√q ≤ 1/5. On the arithmetic quotient the first vector is orthogonal to all Kᵣ-invariant functions. Subtracting its local Kᵣ-average gives a representative with zero mean on each finite fiber. Integrating the finite estimate gives the three angles used in the Hecke norm calculation. The average of the correlation[1613] The index and Cauchy–Schwarz[1614] Distinct lines in the plane[1615] The other index[1616] Fiberwise centering[1617] The three applications[1618]

A calculation at the threshold. In size N = 3 over 𝔽₂₅, the graph at vertex 0 joins points to lines in the projective plane. There are (25³ − 1)/(25 − 1) = 651 points and as many lines. Each line contains 26 points. Give one point value +1, a second point value −1, and all other points zero. Averaging on each line gives +1/26 on the 25 lines through just the first point, −1/26 on the 25 through just the second, and zero elsewhere. The common line cancels. The ratio of output norm to input norm is √(50/26²)/√2 = 5/26. In fact this is the norm on the entire mean-zero subspace. If A is the line-by-point incidence matrix, ATA has diagonal entries 26 and off-diagonal entries 1, since two points determine one line. It acts by 25 on vectors with zero sum. The averaging matrix is A/26. Here the general bound 1/√26 and its uniform relaxation 1/5 both exceed the exact value 5/26. The hypotheses used uniformly in matrix size[1619] The bound retained by the finite-group argument[1620]

Why are the common invariant functions constant?

The Hecke angle estimate applies after the common invariant component has been removed. Work on the common finite cover for the three groups in the flag calculation. Put Eᵢⱼ = Kᵢ ∩ Kⱼ and B = K₀ ∩ K₁ ∩ K₂. A real L² class fixed by all three edge groups Eᵢⱼ is represented almost everywhere by a constant. Since the cover has positive finite volume, a constant with integral zero is zero. In the proof the Hecke average v has integral zero. Its inner product with every such constant vanishes, which places v in the orthogonal complement needed for the angle estimate. The finite-volume setting[1621] The zero integral of the average[1622] The orthogonality actually used[1623]

Which arithmetic group is dense? Write Γ = SLN(𝒪L), where L is totally complex and N ≥ 3. For a prime element π let Dᵣ have its first r diagonal entries equal to π and the rest equal to 1. Then Kᵣ = Dᵣ−1ΓDᵣ inside SLN(L). It is the group generated by K₀ and K₁ whose simultaneous archimedean image is dense in ∏w SLN(ℂ). The norm threshold |𝒪L/(π)| ≥ 25 enters the flag estimate; the density theorem requires only that π be prime. For distinct indices let Tᵢⱼ(a) = I + a eᵢⱼ, with eᵢⱼ the matrix unit. K₀ supplies these transvections for every integral a. Conjugating supplies T0j(1/π) in K₁. With three distinct indices, ordinary matrix multiplication gives

[Tᵢₖ(a), Tₖⱼ(b)] = Tᵢⱼ(ab),   [A,B] = ABA−1B−1.

This multiplies denominators. In the induction from πm to πm+1, use coordinate 0 as the intermediate index for two nonzero endpoints. For a starting index 0, use a third index and the new 1/π on the first factor. For an ending index 0, append an integral transvection to a pair of nonzero endpoints already obtained at the new level. This produces all Tᵢⱼ(a/πm) with integral a. The integral transvections[1627] The first denominator[1628] The commutator calculation[1629] All positions and all powers[1630]

These parameters are dense simultaneously in ∏wℂ. The integer lattice has a finite covering radius R in this product. Given ε > 0, put ε′ = ε/(1 + R). Minkowski’s theorem supplies a nonzero q = y/πm with all |w(q)| < ε/(1 + R). Indeed the volume of the body |w(y)| < ε′|w(π)|m grows in proportion to |Norm π|m, and |Norm π| ≥ 2. Round the tuple (zw/w(q)) to the embeddings of a single algebraic integer a ∈ 𝒪L within distance R. Then aq approximates the whole tuple within ε. By continuity the group closure contains a complex transvection at any one place with identity at the others. Transvections generate SLN(ℂ), giving every factor of the finite product. Two commutators that give a denominator of 49

Take L = ℚ(i), N = 3 and π = 7. The residue field has 49 elements. The first commutator [T₁₀(a), T₀₂(1/7)] gives T₁₂(a/7). The second, [T₀₁(1/7), T₁₂(a/7)], gives T₀₂(a/49). Choose a = 69 + 85i by rounding the coordinates of 49(√2 + i√3). The resulting parameter is within √2/98 of √2 + i√3. This is the one-place version of the simultaneous approximation.

How does density act on an L² class? Choose a measurable, B-invariant representative F of a common class. For each edge group E the finite coset average of F is pointwise E-invariant. Its difference from F has squared norm zero on the cover, so the two agree almost everywhere there. Both are B-invariant, hence the exceptional set is Haar-null in the whole group by the fundamental-domain formula. Left translation preserves null sets. It follows for each γ ∈ E that F(γx) = F(x) for almost every x. The set of γ satisfying this condition is a subgroup, since a translated null set is null. Equality of classes after averaging[1636] Spreading equality from the fundamental domain[1637] Translating a null set[1638] The subgroup of almost-everywhere symmetries[1639]

Why does this subgroup contain both full vertex groups? In K₀ the stabilizer E₀₁ has only one double coset outside itself, by two-transitivity. The index [E₀₂ : B] ≥ 25 supplies an element of E₀₂ outside E₀₁. The subgroup therefore contains that whole double coset and all of K₀. In K₁ use E₁₂ and an element of E₀₁ outside B in the same way. Thus F is invariant almost everywhere under each element of the dense subgroup above. The double-coset argument[1640] Applying it at both vertices[1641]

Why does invariance extend to every translation?

Fix a Borel set U of real values and let T = F−1(U). The translations preserving T up to a null set form a closed set. To see this, take gₙ → g. On a compact test region C, the images gₙC and gC eventually lie in one compact set L₀. The set T ∩ L₀ has finite measure. The measure of the symmetric difference between its two translation preimages tends to zero. If each gₙ preserves T almost everywhere, then g does so on C. A countable compact cover gives the assertion everywhere up to Haar measure zero. Density now gives invariance for every fixed g. Continuity in measure on finite-measure sets[1642] The compact exhaustion[1643]

Such a set has measure zero or has null complement. Indeed, if T has positive measure, Fubini gives a point a ∈ T such that ba ∈ T for almost every b. Right multiplication by a preserves the Haar null sets, so the complement of T is null. Applying this argument to inverse images of a countable family separating real values shows that F is constant almost everywhere. The argument allows the exceptional set to depend on the translation throughout. From sets to real functions[1644] The pinned Haar ergodicity proof[1645]

How the three local bounds of 1/5 give a gap of 3/5

Work in the real Hilbert space of square-integrable coefficients on the common cover. Let P₁, P₂ and P₃ be the orthogonal projections onto the spaces of functions invariant under E₀₁, E₀₂ and E₁₂, respectively. Write Qᵢ = I − Pᵢ for the part lost in this projection. Start with a pair of spaces, and remove from x its projection onto their common subspace. Call the result z. This removal leaves both Qᵢx and Qⱼx unchanged. Write a = Pᵢz, b = Pⱼz and S = ‖a‖² + ‖b‖². The flag estimate gives 2⟨a,b⟩ ≤ S/5. Since S = ⟨z,a + b⟩, Cauchy–Schwarz gives S² ≤ ‖z‖² · (6/5)S. Thus the sum of the two squared losses, T = 2‖z‖² − S, is at least (4/5)‖z‖². From the incidence angle to two projection losses[1646]

Set rᵢ = Qᵢx. For the pair, ⟨rᵢ + rⱼ,z⟩ = T. A second application of Cauchy–Schwarz gives ‖rᵢ + rⱼ‖² ≥ (4/5)T, including the zero case. Sum over all three pairs. Every individual ‖rᵢ‖² occurs twice on the right. On the left the sum of pair squares is ‖∑rᵢ‖² + ∑‖rᵢ‖². Subtraction leaves the factor 2 · (4/5) − 1 = 3/5. In operator notation, for D = ∑Qᵢ, we have ‖Dx‖² ≥ (3/5)⟨Dx,x⟩. Pair inequalities and the three-vector identity[1647] Assembly on the three spaces[1648]

To put the bound on the original coefficient, write E(x) = ⟨Dx,x⟩ = ∑‖Qᵢx‖². Cauchy–Schwarz for the positive form ⟨D·,·⟩ gives ‖Dx‖⁴ ≤ E(x)E(Dx). The preceding estimate now implies E(y) ≥ (3/5)‖y‖² for every y in the range of D. The kernel of D consists of the vectors fixed by all three projections. The common-invariance argument identifies these vectors with the constants. Since D is self-adjoint, its range is dense in their orthogonal complement. Continuity gives the same inequality for every mean-zero coefficient on the cover. The positive-form estimate[1649] Extending the bound from the range[1650] Identifying the kernel[1651]

Where the Hecke factor 3/5 enters

For a prime element whose ideal has norm at least 25 and N ≥ 3, take a continuous, arithmetic- and scalar-invariant real coefficient of mean zero in L². To estimate its Hecke average, lift its translate w and the coset average v of that translate to a common finite cover. Averaging there gives ⟨v,w⟩ = ‖v‖². The angle bound for the invariant subspaces gives |⟨v,w⟩| ≤ (2/5)‖v‖‖w‖. Cancelling ‖v‖ when positive gives a norm bound of 2/5. Both squared norms acquire the same positive covering index, so it cancels on returning to the quotient. The proof weakens 2/5 to 3/5 and preserves mean zero at each step, giving the norm factor (3/5)j after j averages. This is the upper estimate compared with (4/5)j for the stabilized periods. The coefficient hypotheses[1652] The invariant-subspace angle[1653] The averaging identity[1654] Cancellation of the cover index[1655] Passing to 3/5[1656] Iteration[1657]

The average v is orthogonal to the constants. Subtracting the mean of w therefore preserves ⟨v,w⟩, preserves the edge-group invariance of w, and can only decrease its norm. We can now estimate the angle using mean-zero vectors on both sides. The preceding Hilbert-space estimate gives ∑‖(I − Pᵢ)y‖² ≥ (3/5)‖y‖² for every mean-zero y. Take mean-zero unit vectors u fixed by P₁ and P₂, and z fixed by P₁ and P₃, choosing the sign so t = ⟨u,z⟩ ≥ 0. For y = u + z the first error is zero. Since ⟨u,P₂z⟩ = t, the second error has square 1 − ‖P₂z‖² ≤ 1 − t². The third has the same bound. Thus (3/5)·2(1 + t) ≤ 2(1 − t²). Cancelling 2(1 + t) gives t ≤ 2/5. The pairwise 1/5 hypothesis from coset averaging[1658] The complementary projections[1653] The quadratic inequality for the angle[1659]

How can the mean of the coefficients define a form at every point?

The previous average over central scalars produced a form ω′ with the original periods. Now we want a form invariant under every archimedean matrix. Let G = ∏w GLN(ℂ), let S = ∏w SLN(ℂ), and write Agh = (g−1)*h g−1 for their action on Hermitian matrices. The tangent spaces of the positive cone are copies of the same real vector space. At y ∈ S pull the form at AyI back to the identity. This gives an alternating multilinear form F(y) = ω′(AyI) ∘ Ay, with Ay applied to each tangent argument. It is left invariant under the arithmetic subgroup Λ = SLN(𝒪L′) in its archimedean embedding. Let D be a fundamental domain for Λ in S of positive finite Haar volume. The height moment makes F square-integrable there, hence integrable. We can now take an ordinary vector-valued mean in a fixed space. The moving frame and the form action[1660] The hypotheses and the proposed mean[1661] From the moment to integrability[1662]

M = (vol D)−1 ∫D F(y) dy,   ω̄(AgI) = M ∘ Ag−1.
Why do two matrices taking the identity to the same point give the same answer?

The ambiguity at the identity is a tuple of unitary matrices u. At each place choose a unit-modulus Nth root of det u and divide by it. The resulting k belongs to S and acts exactly like u on Hermitian matrices. Hence F(y) ∘ Au = F(yk). Right translation by k preserves Haar measure on S. It also carries a fundamental domain to another one, since it commutes with left multiplication by Λ. Integrating a Λ-invariant integrable function over either domain gives the same integral. This proves M ∘ Au = M. Every positive Hermitian tuple can be written AgI by factoring each matrix in the tuple as B*B and choosing g = B−1. Two choices differ on the right by a stabilizer of I. The displayed transport rule therefore gives a single value at every point. The group law then makes ω̄ invariant under all of G, with constant moving-frame coefficients M. Right shifts of the domain[1663] Removing the unitary determinant[1664] Invariance of the mean under the stabilizer[1665] Reaching every positive matrix[1666] Transport independent of all choices[1667]

Check it on a matrix. For one complex place and degree one take M(V) = tr(V). Unitary conjugation preserves this real functional on Hermitian matrices. At h = AgI the transported value on V is tr(g*Vg) = tr(h−1V). For h = diag(4,9) and V = diag(4,0) it equals 1. Taking the upper-left entry instead would already fail at h = I. Both the identity and the coordinate swap carry I to itself, but on diag(1,0) they give 1 and 0.

Subtract ω̄ from ω′. Each scalar coefficient of the remainder now has integral zero on D, since evaluation on fixed tangent vectors commutes with the mean. This is the conclusion that the Hecke estimate needs. Equality of the periods of ω̄ and ω′ still requires the two decay estimates on stabilized cycles. How does a bound in L² control the period of one cycle?

A low-dimensional simplex can have zero volume in the surrounding space. An L² estimate on the ambient quotient therefore gives no direct estimate for restriction to that simplex. What makes the argument work here is that a closed cycle has the same period after its vertices are averaged. The resulting integral can be estimated using ambient volume.

Fix a finite bar cycle z of degree m ≥ 1 in GLN(𝒪L′). Write F(y₀,…,ym) for the integral of the form ω on the affine simplex with those vertices in the cone of positive Hermitian matrices. The proof assumes that F is invariant under the arithmetic group and that its alternating sum over the faces of every (m + 1)-simplex vanishes. For a bar symbol [g₁|…|gm], set h₀ = 1 and hj = g₁⋯gj. Choose independent points Y₀,…,Ym with normalized volume on a closed ball about the identity matrix I, small enough to lie inside the cone. Then

⟨ω,z⟩ = ∑g z(g) · 𝔼[F(h₀·Y₀,…,hm·Ym)].

To see why, allow each vertex to carry one of two marks, “fixed at I” or “averaged.” Removing a vertex leaves the same product probability law on the others. The alternating face sum of the marked cochain is therefore the expectation of a face sum of F, hence zero. The prism between the two choices of basepoint has coboundary equal to the difference between all-averaged and all-fixed evaluations. On z this difference is zero because ∂z = 0. The marked cocycle and the two evaluations[1671] Prism identity on a cycle[1560]

A one-dimensional check. Let ℤ act on ℝ by translations, put P(x) = x + sin(2πx), and take F(x,y) = P(y) − P(x). Integer translation leaves F unchanged and its three face terms telescope. The bar cycle [2] has period F(0,2) = 2. Take independent Y₀,Y₁ uniform on {0,1/4}. The four values of F(Y₀,2 + Y₁) are 2, 13/4, 3/4 and 2. Their mean is 2. This discrete example checks the averaging identity. The volume estimate uses the ball with its continuous distribution.

For that estimate, fix a bar symbol. Let Aj be the invertible real linear action of hj on the ambient Hermitian space of real dimension d. A point of the random simplex is ∑j τjAjYj, with nonnegative barycentric coordinates summing to one. Some τi ≥ 1/(m + 1). Hold all the other vertices fixed. Changing variables in Yi gives a density bounded by (m + 1)d/(vol(B) |det Ai|), where B is the ball. The edge lengths are uniformly bounded and the possible simplex points fill a compact set K inside the cone. Integrating in the simplex parameters now bounds the expected absolute simplex integral by a constant times ∫K ‖ω‖. Central-scalar invariance lets the proof unfold this last integral into a bound by the integral of the moving-frame norm ‖fr ω‖ on a compact set K′ inside ∏w SLN(ℂ). Write Λ for the image of SLN(𝒪L′) and D for its fundamental domain. If λ₀x and λx both belong to K′, then λλ₀⁻¹ lies in the finite set Λ ∩ K′(K′)⁻¹. Its cardinality bounds the number of visits from any one orbit. Arithmetic invariance therefore bounds the integral on K′ by this cardinality times ∫D ‖fr ω‖. Cauchy–Schwarz supplies the last factor vol(D)1/2 ‖fr ω‖2. Summing over the finite support of z with weights |z(g)| gives a constant Cz independent of the form. |⟨Hjω₀,z⟩| ≤ Cz √(KbasisS₀) (3/5)j.

Where the lower factor 4/5 comes from

Let In and IN be the numbers of cosets in the respective Hecke averages and put α = In/IN. The cosets inherited from size n contribute α times a smaller-size Hecke period vector yj. For the other cosets, transfer from their stabilizers gives the original periods after summing. Thus xj+1 = (1 − α)xj + αyj. The smaller-size operator acts linearly on a finite-dimensional space of period vectors, so ‖yj‖ ≤ K‖xj‖ with K independent of N and j. Since IN ≥ N, we can arrange α(1 + K) ≤ 1/5. The reverse triangle inequality now gives ‖xj+1‖ ≥ (1 − α(1 + K))‖xj‖ ≥ (4/5)‖xj‖. For example, if ‖x₀‖ were 1 and the upper constant were 2, three iterations would require 64/125 ≤ ‖x₃‖ ≤ 54/125. Which cosets carry the original period into the next Hecke average?

Write ΓN = GLN(𝒪L′), q = diag(π,1,…,1) and k = 𝒪L′/(π). A matrix γ lies in the subgroup SN that labels the Hecke cosets precisely when qγq−1 is integral and invertible over the integers. Conjugation divides the first column below its top entry by π and multiplies the rest of the first row by π. The determinant stays a unit. Thus membership is equivalent to preserving the line ke₁ modulo π. For a right coset SNc, take the residue line of c−1e₁. Two representatives determine the same line exactly when they determine the same coset. There are finitely many such lines, and swapping the first coordinate with each coordinate realizes N distinct lines. In particular the index IN is at least N. A coset inherited from Γn has all its last r coordinates zero on this line. Conversely, if those coordinates vanish, some coordinate in the first block is nonzero. Swap it into first position. Over k, subtract multiples of the first row to clear the other entries. These row additions lift to invertible integral operations in size n. The resulting line is ke₁, so the original coset came from the smaller group. Stabilization identifies its cosets bijectively with this part of the larger sum. The smaller group permutes the complementary set X of cosets by right multiplication. Here the nonzero coordinate in the last block matters. It permits a change of basis in which the translated stabilizer acts by integral matrices with diagonal blocks h and 1 and only one possible off-diagonal block above them. To pass from a stabilizer to the whole group, choose one representative x₀ per orbit. xj+1 = (1 − In/IN) xj + (In/IN) yj.

f∗z − (D ∘ f₀)∗z = ∂y.

A unit square distinguishes the two orders

Take the coordinate characters x, y on ℤ², with unit vectors u, v in that order. The bar simplex [a|b] has vertices 0, a, a + b. Its boundary is [b] − [a + b] + [a]. Thus z = [u|v] − [v|u] is a cycle. On its two triangles x ∪ y has successive values 1 and 0, so it evaluates to 1 on z. Reversing the characters gives 0 and 1, hence −1 on z. Every coboundary evaluates to zero on this cycle, so the first cup represents a nonzero class.

In the affine argument a separate eigenvalue calculation supplies a polynomial Fj that kills each cup word under pullback by multiplication by a chosen unit v. The split extension A → P → Γn gives cochains with a horizontal differential in the quotient variables and a vertical differential in the group variables. A prism between translation and conjugation shows that Fj(R) of the cochain is vertically exact, by the polynomial calculation on the kernel. A horizontal prism shows that R − 1 is horizontally exact on this cochain. In the first column the horizontal translation fixes the cochain and the vertical coboundary alone suffices. Write S = s ∘ p. Subtracting the pullback by S gives c − S∗c = δ(e − S∗e), since pS = p. Thus every real cocycle evaluates to zero on w − S∗w for a cycle w of P. Both satisfy X² − X − 1 = 0, a smaller annihilating polynomial whose value at 1 is −1. Write U(b) = [[1,b],[0,1]] and D = diag(v,1). Direct multiplication gives DU(v)D−1U(v)−1 = U(v²−v) = U(1). Why does one trace per complex place suffice on the filtered cycles?

The transported mean gives a form ω invariant under every archimedean change of basis. To integrate it on a homology class, we first need its integral to vanish on boundaries. Write M = ω(I) for its value at the identity tuple and Y₁,…,Ym for Hermitian tangent vectors. All matrix operations below are taken place by place. For a positive Hermitian tuple x, the matrix g = x−1 takes I to x², and sends Y to xYx. Invariance therefore gives ω(x²)(xY₁x,…,xYmx) = M(Y₁,…,Ym). Near I the squaring map has a smooth inverse because its derivative is twice the identity. Solving this formula for ω by undoing each tangent map gives smoothness near I. The matrix action in this identity[1734] The local inverse and smoothness[1735]

DωI[X](Y₁,…,Ym) = −½ ∑j=1m M(Y₁,…,XYj + YjX,…,Ym).

To obtain the derivative, put x = I + tX in the preceding identity. The base point moves with velocity 2X and the jth argument with velocity XYj + YjX. The right side is constant. To obtain the exterior derivative, alternate the left side of the displayed formula in its m + 1 inputs. Swapping X and the selected Yj preserves their sum of products and reverses the sign. Every term cancels. Invariance carries dω = 0 from I to every positive tuple. Stokes’ theorem now makes the integral of ω over the boundary of every affine simplex zero. Its periods therefore descend to homology. The two Hecke estimates then show that the transported mean has the periods of the original detecting cocycle. Count the independent block labels. At I, M is invariant under unitary conjugation at each place. The tensor invariant theorem expresses it as a real linear combination of alternating real or imaginary parts of products of traces. Each product is indexed by a permutation of the m inputs. A cycle (i₁ … iℓ) contributes tr(Yi₁,w ⋯ Yiℓ,w) at a single place w. This trace sums over matrix indices around a closed loop. Replace each matrix by d identical diagonal blocks. A nonzero matrix entry must stay within one block, so the entire loop chooses a single block in d ways. With j permutation cycles there are dj choices. This is the weight j of the period under block repetition. The invariant tensor span and alternation[1739] Counting block labels by permutation cycles[1740] Passing the scaling law to periods[1741]

In odd degree m, a single cycle orders all the matrices at one place. Relabeling the inputs of its alternating trace changes only the sign. Reversing their order conjugates the trace because each matrix is Hermitian. Reversal has sign (−1)m(m−1)/2, so the alternating trace is real for m ≡ 1 modulo 4 and purely imaginary for m ≡ 3 modulo 4. This leaves at most one real functional per place. The filter on the selected cycles kills every weight from 2 to m. Any surviving invariant period is thus a linear combination of these r₂ one-place evaluations. A nonzero filtered homology class has a detecting period, which gives the rank bound. Why do these trace products span all invariant tensors?

After allowing complex scalars, the tensor at the identity is represented by a matrix T acting on a tensor power. Unitary invariance says that T commutes with every tensor power of a placewise unitary matrix. Consider the operators that permute the tensor slots and select a place in each slot. The first finite-dimensional matrix result says that every operator commuting with all of them is a linear combination of those unitary tensor powers. Thus T commutes with all such operators. The second matrix result says that this puts T itself in the span of the slot permutations with place selections. In one such term, a matrix entry links index ai to aπ(i). Summing around each cycle gives its trace. If the place changes across a link, the entry vanishes. Taking real parts and alternating recovers the real tensor M. To recover the invariant forms, we need the matrices T that commute with every such operator. The proof works for all finite block sizes N and tensor degrees q, including N < q. It gives a spanning family whose members can coincide in small dimension. From a Hermitian form to a commuting matrix[1748]

A basis index I is a word of q pairs (place, coordinate). For a place pattern w = (w₁,…,wq) and a permutation σ, define Pσ,w by its rows and columns.

(Pσ,w)I,J = 1 if place(Ii) = wi for every i and J = I ∘ σ, and 0 otherwise.

These matrices commute with every D⊗q. Indeed, a block unitary preserves the place pattern and the same D acts in every slot. Let 𝒜 be their complex span and 𝒰 the span of the unitary tensor powers. Write 𝒮′ for the matrices commuting with all of 𝒮. The archive proves 𝒜′ ⊆ 𝒰 by interpolation and 𝒜″ ⊆ 𝒜 by orthogonal projection. Thus 𝒰′ = 𝒜. If Z commutes with the projections Pid,w, its entry ZI,J can be nonzero only if the places of I and J agree slot by slot. Commuting with all the other Pσ,w gives ZI∘σ,J∘σ = ZI,J. If EI,J denotes a matrix unit, expand Z in these units and sum over slot permutations. The resulting identity counts each permutation, including those fixing an index pair. q! Z = ∑I,J ZI,J ∑σ EI∘σ,J∘σ.

Suppose a complex linear functional φ vanishes on 𝒰. For any block diagonal D, we claim φ(D⊗q) = 0. Start with Hermitian blocks and fix their unitary eigenbases. As the diagonal eigenvalues vary, the expression is polynomial of degree at most q in each variable. It vanishes on the grid where every diagonal entry is a (q + 1)st root of unity, because every resulting block is unitary. Interpolating in one variable at a time gives vanishing at the actual eigenvalues. Now write arbitrary blocks as H + iK with H, K Hermitian. Fix an ambient size b and put G = Γb(R). An ordered split sequence of length p is a list of vectors and covectors (v₁,λ₁), …, (vp,λp) with λi(vj) = δij. Write Cp for the free abelian group on these sequences. The group acts on the vectors by g and on the covectors by precomposition with g−1. The differential dp from Cp+1 to Cp deletes one pair with alternating signs. The empty sequence gives C₀ = ℤ. When p + s ≤ b, the action is transitive. The stabilizer of the last p standard vector–covector pairs is diag(Γb−p,Ip). Fixing both the vectors and the covectors forces the two off-diagonal blocks to vanish. Shapiro’s lemma for this permutation module therefore identifies Hq(G,Cp) with Hq(Γb−p,ℤ). When p + 1 + s ≤ b, both consecutive identifications are isomorphisms. In these coordinates each deletion gives the same stabilization map. A permutation of the final coordinates arranges the remaining pairs in standard order and commutes with Γb−p−1. The sum of p + 1 alternating signs is one for even p and zero for odd p. A split pair in Rn is a vector v with a specified linear functional λ satisfying λ(v) = 1. An ordered list of pairs is split if λi(vj) = δij. Write Cp for the free abelian group on such lists of length p. Its boundary deletes one pair at a time, starting with sign +. How an integral boundary matrix bounds torsion

The character count above uses the orders of the torsion subgroups of two integral homology groups. A torsion class is killed by a nonzero integer. An infinite free summand in homology can therefore coexist with the finite quantity we need to bound. Start with a free lattice E = ℤr, with r ≤ A, and any set of integral relation vectors. Write Λ for their integer span. Suppose each relation has sum of absolute coordinates at most b, where b ≥ 1. The bound used in the proof is

|tors(E/Λ)| ≤ bA.

If we have r independent relation vectors, put them in a square matrix V. The sublattice they generate has index |det V|. Expanding the determinant as a signed sum over permutations and taking absolute values gives a sum of products. Allowing every choice of one column for each row only increases this sum, and the enlarged sum factors as ∏i ∑j |Vij|. This proves the bound br. Additional relations give a quotient of this finite group. Permutation expansion and row sums[1837] Lattice index from the determinant[1838]

Suppose instead that the relation vectors span only a proper rational subspace. Choose a maximal independent subset and complete it to a rational basis using standard unit vectors. Let K be the integer span of that completed list. Its determinant still has absolute value at most br, since every added vector has length one. To compare torsion, choose a lift in E for each torsion class in E/Λ and reduce its lift modulo K. If two images coincide, the difference x of their lifts lies in K. Their difference class is torsion, so some nonzero multiple of x belongs to Λ. Consequently x lies in the rational span of the original relations. In the completed basis every coefficient of an added vector must then vanish. Because x belongs to K, the remaining coefficients are integers. Thus x is an integer combination of selected relations and the two classes were equal. This injects the set of torsion classes into the finite set E/K. In the first two coordinates a vector is a relation exactly when the coordinates have the same parity. Hence the torsion subgroup has order two. Choosing the first two relations and the third unit vector gives det V = 4. The general bound gives 2³ = 8. The three numbers measure respectively the actual torsion, the index for this completed list, and the estimate using the common row bound.

Find a frame shared by the whole face

For each infinite place of F take a Hermitian form on ℂN. Their values on the images of a lattice vector y add to a real number qh(y). Impose qh(y) ≥ 1 for every nonzero y. The common minimal vectors of a face span FN. To see why, average the vertices. At the average a lattice inequality is tight exactly when it is tight at every vertex. If the common minimal vectors missed a direction, a nonzero F-linear functional λ would vanish on their span. The family of rank-one forms obtained from |λ|² at all embeddings is positive semidefinite and nonzero. A sufficiently small subtraction of this family from the average preserves the tight constraints. Local finiteness of the inequalities keeps the others feasible. The supporting functional would strictly decrease below its minimum. Thus we can choose N independent common minimal columns and place them in a matrix A. They form a basis over F. Its integral determinant can be a nonunit. The determinant estimate gives

r = |NormF/ℚ(det A)| ≤ J,   J = DNdd.

For this last inequality the source pulls each local form back by A. The pulled-back determinants have product at most one by the diagonal bounds and Hadamard’s inequality. Their product is r times the product of the original determinants, for which the geometric lower bound is 1/J. An element fixing an ordered tuple fixes its first vertex. The first vertex has finitely many minimal vectors, and these include N independent ones. Which ideal does the cyclotomic element generate?

At level N = Fd, the auxiliary function construction starts with a number Xd in KN = ℚ(μN). We first construct it at a single level, then compare the choices at N and qN. Write σt for the automorphism sending an Nth root to its tth power, c = σ−1 for complex conjugation, and [t]N for the representative between 0 and N − 1. For an integral ideal 𝔞 write 𝔞t = σt−1(𝔞). θN(t) = ⌊b[t]N/N⌋ − ⌊b[−t]N/N⌋,   (X) = ∏t∈(ℤ/Nℤ)× 𝔞tθN(t),   Xc(X) = 1.

For every N ≥ 1, 0 ≤ b < N and nonzero integral ideal 𝔞 of KN, the proof produces a nonzero field element X with these two properties. A negative exponent means that the prime ideal occurs in the denominator of a fractional ideal. The original ideal 𝔞 can lie in any ideal class. How a finite-field sum gives the signed ideal powers

Begin with a prime ideal P of residue degree one above a rational prime p ∤ N. Reduction π identifies its residue field with 𝔽p. The primitive Nth roots retain their order on reduction, so N divides p − 1. Put h = (p − 1)/N and lift x ↦ xh from 𝔽p× to its character χ of order N with values in μN. For 1 ≤ j < b, let Jj = ∑x∈𝔽p χ(x)χj(1 − x), extending the characters by zero at zero. Set J = ∏1≤j<bJj. Our candidate for P is XP = c(J)/J. Each Jacobi sum here divides p, so it is nonzero, and the prime factors of its ideal occur with exponent at most one since (p) splits without multiplicity. Selecting the inverse class and the character[2082] The Jacobi product for the split prime[2084] Jacobi-sum divisibility input[2085] Factorization of the rational prime[2086] From membership to multiplicity one[2087]

Which character takes values in the cyclotomic integers?

The Jacobi identity multiplies two algebraic integers. A sum computed only modulo p would lose the ideal it is supposed to measure. Let K = ℚ(ζ), where ζ has order M ≥ 1, and choose a prime ideal of norm p with p ∤ M. Its quotient has p elements. Identify it with 𝔽p and call the resulting reduction π. The algebraic integer ζ satisfies the cyclotomic polynomial ΦM. Its reduction satisfies the same polynomial modulo p. As p ∤ M, the roots of XM − 1 are simple, and the cyclotomic factors for the divisors of M have disjoint roots. A root of ΦM therefore has exact order M. In particular πζ has that order and M divides p − 1. The prime-norm quotient[2088] Reducing a primitive root[2089] The reduction chosen in the construction[2090]

Put h = (p − 1)/M. For each nonzero x in 𝔽p, the element xh is an Mth root of unity. The M powers of πζ are distinct and list every such root. Find the exponent 0 ≤ a < M with xh = (πζ)a and set χ(x) = ζa. Set χ(0) = 0. Multiplying two residues adds their exponents modulo M, so χ is multiplicative. Its order is exactly M. Indeed, if χk = 1, a generator g of 𝔽p× satisfies ghk = 1 after reduction. Hence Mh divides hk, so M divides k. Conversely all nonzero values have Mth power one. This explains why the nontriviality checks on the Jacobi characters reduce to exponent checks. Existence and uniqueness of each lifted root[2091] Multiplication and the upper order bound[2092] Testing on a generator[2093] The character condition in the Jacobi construction[2094]

Lift the residue 2 at level five

Take M = 5 and p = 11, with πζ = 3. The powers of 3 starting at exponent zero are 1, 3, 9, 5, 4 and then 1. Since h = 2, square the input 2 to obtain 4. The required lift is χ(2) = ζ⁴. Squaring this value gives χ(4) = ζ³. Checking the other way, 4² ≡ 5 ≡ 3³ modulo 11. For the other reduction π′ζ = 9, the input 2 still gives 2² = 4. Since 9² ≡ 4 modulo 11, its lift is now χ′(2) = ζ². The prime ideal is part of the construction.

Why every prime above p occurs only once

For each invertible residue t modulo M let σt(ζ) = ζt and put Pt = ker(π ∘ σt). This inverse-image convention is what sets the indices in the signed divisor. Every reduction is onto, since ordinary integers already give all of 𝔽p. Its kernel is therefore a maximal ideal of norm p. If two kernels agreed, subtract from any algebraic integer the ordinary integer representing its first reduction. The difference would also belong to the second kernel, forcing both reductions to agree on that element. Applying this to ζ gives (πζ)s = (πζ)t, hence s = t. Distinct kernels from one primitive root[2095] Norm and maximality[2096]

These φ(M) distinct maximal ideals are pairwise coprime, and each divides (p). Their product divides (p) and already has norm pφ(M). This equals the norm of (p), because [K : ℚ] = φ(M). The leftover integral ideal has norm one and is the unit ideal. Thus (p) = ∏tPt. For a Jacobi sum J dividing p, this gives ordPₜ(J) ∈ {0,1}. Testing π(σtJ) = 0 tells exactly which exponent is one. In the example at 11 the four reductions send ζ to 3, 9, 5 and 4. A repeated prime would exhaust too much of the norm. The product divides the principal ideal[2097] Equality of norms[2098] Recovering the subset by ideal membership[2099] Application to each Jacobi factor[2087]

To tell which primes occur, reduce σt(Jj) modulo P. The result is ∑ xA(1 − x)B with A = h[t]N and B = h[jt]N. Both exponents lie strictly between 0 and p − 1. Expand the binomial. In degree A + k the sum of powers over the field vanishes unless p − 1 divides the degree. Since all degrees are positive and below 2(p − 1), only k = p − 1 − A can contribute. When this index is in the expansion its binomial coefficient is nonzero modulo p, since B < p. Thus the residue is zero exactly when A + B < p − 1, or [t]N + [jt]N < N. Each addition without a carry contributes one factor of Pt to (J). Reducing each conjugate of a Jacobi sum[2100] The finite-field power-sum calculation[2101] The surviving binomial coefficient[2102] From membership to multiplicity one[2087]

Let e(t) count these additions. For b ≥ 1 there are b − 1 steps. The number of carries is ⌊b[t]N/N⌋, since each new addition increases the integer quotient by one precisely when a carry occurs. Hence e(t) = b − 1 − ⌊b[t]N/N⌋. Conjugation exchanges Pt and P−t, so the exponent in (c(J)/J) is e(−t) − e(t) = θN(t). The product with its complex conjugate is 1 by cancellation. At b = 0 the Jacobi product is empty and XP = 1, as all the floor weights vanish. Summing the carries[2103] Swapping the two exponents under conjugation[2104] The signed ideal exponent of the quotient[2105]

Compute a denominator at level 5

Take N = 5, b = 3 and p = 11, so h = 2. At t = 1 the Jacobi factors for j = 1,2 give exponents (A,B) = (2,2),(2,4). Both sums vanish modulo 11 because their degrees stay below 10. At t = 4 the pairs are (8,8),(8,6). Both reach degree 10. The surviving terms give −28 ≡ 5 and −15 ≡ 7 modulo 11. Thus e(1) = 2 and e(4) = 0. The quotient c(J)/J has exponent −2 at P1, +2 at P4, and 0 at the other two primes. This agrees with θ5(1) = ⌊3/5⌋ − ⌊12/5⌋ = −2.

Why each Jacobi sum divides the split prime

The cyclotomic construction determines a signed ideal by testing a product of Jacobi sums at the primes above p. A zero residue proves that one such prime divides a factor. How can we tell that its square does not? Each factor has an explicit partner whose product with it is p. At a split unramified prime, the order of p is one, so the nonnegative orders of the two partners sum to one. This turns the residue test into an exact exponent. Using divisibility in the ideal factorization[2087] Applying it separately to each factor[2084]

Let χ and φ be multiplicative characters of 𝔽p× taking values in a characteristic-zero integral domain R, extended by zero at zero. Assume χ, φ and χφ are all nontrivial. Define J(χ,φ) = ∑x∈𝔽pχ(x)φ(1−x). The partner uses the inverse of each character. Its values already lie in R, since every nonzero character value is a unit. The ring-valued divisibility statement[2106]

J(χ,φ) J(χ−1,φ−1) = p.

To compute the product, pass to the fraction field of R and then to a cyclotomic extension containing a nontrivial additive character ψ of 𝔽p. Write Gψ(ρ) = ∑xρ(x)ψ(x). In the product Gψ(χ)Gψ(φ), group pairs (x,y) by t = x+y. At t = 0 their total is φ(−1)∑x(χφ)(x) = 0. At t ≠ 0 put x = tu. The two characters contribute (χφ)(t)χ(u)φ(1−u). Summing yields Gψ(χφ)J(χ,φ). Regrouping the finite double sum[2107] Choosing the additive character in an extension[2108]

A second orthogonality identity says Gψ(ρ)Gψ−1(ρ−1) = p for nontrivial ρ. To see why, expand the two sums and put x = uy for y ≠ 0. At each y the summand becomes ρ(u)ψ(y(u−1)). We can include y = 0 because its total is ∑uρ(u) = 0. Summing over all y now leaves only u = 1, contributing p. Apply the first identity twice, once with ψ and once with its inverse and the inverse multiplicative characters. Multiplication and the second identity give pJ(χ,φ)J(χ−1,φ−1) = p². Cancelling p and using injectivity of the two field embeddings gives the claimed identity in R. See the two factors of 7 in the Eisenstein integers

Take the level M = 3, b = 2 and p = 7. In ℤ[ω], with ω²+ω+1 = 0, choose the cubic character determined by χ(3) = ω, since 3 generates 𝔽₇×. At the prime where ω reduces to 2 it satisfies the required reduction χ(x) ≡ x². Here the Jacobi product has one factor, J(χ,χ). The inputs 0 and 1 contribute zero. For x = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 the five contributions are ω², 1, ω², 1, ω². The sum and its inverse-character partner are 2+3ω² and 2+3ω. Their product is 4+6(ω+ω²)+9 = 7. At ω ≡ 2 modulo 7 the first is zero and the second is one. At ω ≡ 4 their roles reverse. Each factor has order exactly one at the prime where it vanishes. The reduction required of the lifted character[2111] Where the level and index enter[2084]

In the application the two characters are χ and χj with 1 ≤ j < b < M. The reduction hypothesis gives χ order M, so the exponents 1, j and 1+j meet all three nontriviality conditions. Multiplication of the individually factored ideals then adds their prime orders. These cyclotomic elements enter the reciprocity construction behind the minus character estimate. The Bernoulli denominator calculation makes the character factors integral when their valuations are added across primes.
