Passing from a prime to any ideal class
How to choose the prime in the inverse ideal class

The Jacobi sum uses a prime ideal P whose residue field has a prime number of elements. To apply that calculation to an arbitrary nonzero integral ideal 𝔞, the same P must make 𝔞P principal. For a prime of a number field K above a rational prime p, its absolute norm NP is the residue field size pf. Thus absolute residue degree one means NP = p. We can require this degree, prescribe the ideal class [P] = c and exclude any finite set of prime ideals of K. The degree over the rational residue field[2114] The prime selected in an ideal class[2115]

Let H be the Hilbert class field of K. Its Artin isomorphism sends [P] to the arithmetic Frobenius at a prime above P, acting on residues by x ↦ xNP. Apply the degree-one prime theorem to H/K with target automorphism Art(c). The Frobenius supplied by the theorem restricts to this precise automorphism. Two Frobenius lifts at the same place agree modulo inertia, and inertia in H/K is trivial. Applying Art−1 gives [P] = c. In the cyclotomic application take c = [𝔞]−1 and exclude the primes dividing N𝒪K, where N is the cyclotomic level. This set is finite because N ≠ 0. Then p ∤ N, reduction preserves the order of ζN, and N divides p − 1 as the character construction requires. The inverse on [𝔞] comes from [𝔞][P] = 1. The Artin convention[1227] Comparing the Frobenius lifts[2116] The exclusions and the inverse class[2082]

How can the proof still impose absolute degree one?

Write L/K for the finite Galois extension and g for the requested automorphism. The proof chooses an auxiliary prime ℓ with [L : K] dividing ℓ − 1 and Φℓ irreducible over L. In L(ζℓ) choose an automorphism h restricting to g on L and raising ζℓ to a generator τ of (ℤ/ℓℤ)×. Irreducibility permits this choice by adjusting a lift of g with an automorphism fixing L. Take the fixed field Z of ⟨h⟩ inside this compositum. The powers of h realize every exponent on ζℓ, so Φℓ is still irreducible over Z. Choosing the auxiliary prime[2117] Constructing the fixed field[2118]

Above the finite exclusions and the ramified primes of L/K there are only finitely many primes of Z. Away from these, seek a prime w with Nw ≡ τ modulo ℓ. A prime-distribution result gives divergence of the sum of reciprocal prime-ideal norms in this residue class. Primes of absolute degree at least two contribute at most [Z : ℚ]∑p primep−2, since at most [Z : ℚ] primes of Z lie above each p. The finite exclusions also contribute a finite amount. Hence a remaining w has prime norm p. For P below w, the equality Nw = (NP)f(w/P) forces NP = p. The reciprocal sum and what can be discarded[2119] Where the finite exclusions enter[2120] Descending a prime norm[2121]

A Frobenius lift at w fixes Z and acts on the ℓth roots by the pth power, since p ≠ ℓ and those roots remain distinct after reduction. Its action in the compositum is therefore hj with τj = τ. Thus j ≡ 1 modulo ℓ − 1. The order of g divides [L : K], which divides ℓ − 1, so gj = g. The equality of norms lets the same lift serve as an arithmetic Frobenius at P. Recovering the chosen automorphism[2122] Passing from residues to roots of unity[2123]

See the inverse class in a quadratic field

In ℚ(√−23) let ω = (1 + √−23)/2, so ω² − ω + 6 = 0. Exclude the primes above 2 and start with 𝔞 = (2,ω). Taking P = (3,ω) gives residue field 𝔽₃. The two ideals are coprime and both divide (ω). Their norms 2 and 3 multiply to N(ω) = 6, hence 𝔞P = (ω). Here the inverse class is genuinely different. The norm form a² + ab + 6b² never takes the value 2, so 𝔞 is nonprincipal. The element ω − 2 has norm 8 and is nonzero modulo the other prime (2,ω − 1) above 2, giving (ω − 2) = 𝔞³. Thus [𝔞] has order three and [P] = [𝔞]².

Given 𝔞, choose a degree-one prime P outside the primes dividing N, in the inverse ideal class [𝔞]−1. The source obtains it by applying degree-one Chebotarev in the Hilbert class field. Now 𝔞P = (y) for a nonzero algebraic integer y. For a principal ideal the formula is immediate. Put Z(y) = ∏t σt−1(y)θN(t). Its ideal has the required factors for (y), and pairing t with −t gives Z(y)c(Z(y)) = 1 by antisymmetry. Divide this element by XP. At each conjugate prime the factors contributed by P cancel, leaving exactly the fractional ideal prescribed for 𝔞. The identity with complex conjugation survives division. Degree-one primes in a chosen ideal class[2115] Selecting the inverse class and the character[2082] Dividing out the auxiliary prime[2083] Principal-ideal formula and division rule[2124]

How much does the choice of generator matter? If X and X′ solve the same problem, their quotient w generates the unit ideal. It is an algebraic unit, and wc(w) = 1. Under every complex embedding this says |w| = 1. Kronecker’s theorem then makes w a root of unity. The torsion order of the units in KN divides 2N, hence w2N = 1. Both conditions on the generator enter this argument. For example, (3 + 4i)/5 in ℚ(i) has complex absolute value one, but its trace 6/5 rules out integrality. The quotient is a unit of absolute value one[2125] The cyclotomic torsion exponent[2126]

What happens to the exponents under the norm?

Let q be a prime with q ∤ N, and let u be its residue modulo N. For b < q, sum the weights of the units upstairs lying over a fixed t downstairs. Among the q possible lifts [t]N + iN, exactly one is divisible by q, namely q[u−1t]N. Its missing floor is ⌊b[u−1t]N/N⌋. Summing before removing that lift gives ⌊b[t]N/N⌋ plus a constant independent of t. For 0 < b < q, this follows because the residues ib run once through all residues modulo q. Taking the difference at t and −t cancels the constant. At b = 0 both sides vanish. The missing multiple of q and the floor distribution[2127]

∑t′ ↦ t θqN(t′) = θN(t) − θN(u−1t).

Take a nonzero ideal 𝔞′ upstairs and elements X′ and X satisfying the two defining conditions for 𝔞′ and its relative norm downstairs. The field norm of X′ multiplies its conjugates over KN. Grouping the factors of their ideals by the fibres t′ ↦ t gives the sum on the left. On the right the first weight is the exponent for X and the second gives the exponent for σu−1(X). The principal fractional ideals of the field norm and of X/σu−1(X) therefore coincide. Both generators have product one with their complex conjugates, so their quotient is a root ξn in the smaller field with ξn2N = 1. Field norm and shifted denominator[2128] Comparing the ideal exponents on each fibre[2129] The root in the smaller field[2130]

One root for every place above the new prime

Assume also b < N and that 𝔞′ is coprime to (q). The congruence compares X′ to the image of σu−1(X) at every prime over q using one root ξc in KqN. Here is how the proof keeps that root independent of the place. One root for every place over q[2131] A second inverse-class prime outside qN[2132]

  1. For a split auxiliary prime P away from qN, choose residue characters χ′ and χ for the two levels. Their defining exponents imply (χ′)q = χ after embedding downstairs into the larger field. At a place over q, the residue field has characteristic q, so its qth-power map is injective. There χ′ reduces to the same value as σu−1χ, since taking the qth power gives χ for both. The Jacobi products and their conjugates compare term by term. Their denominators are units at q since their factors divide p ≠ q. Passing from these explicit Jacobi elements to other solutions introduces the ratio of the two uniqueness roots. That ratio is chosen before any place over q. Matching the two residue characters[2133] · Comparing Jacobi products at every place[2134]
  2. For a principal ideal (y) coprime to (q), the product Z′(y) has the same residue as σu−1Z(Norm y). To see the use of the floor formula, let f(t) be the residue of a conjugate σt′−1y upstairs, where t′ lies over t. The lifts agree on μN and every qth root of unity reduces to 1 in residue characteristic q, so all lifts give the same residue. Frobenius gives f(t) = f(ut)q. Each value is nonzero. Using the distribution formula, the new product becomes ∏t [f(t)/f(ut)]θN(t) = ∏t f(ut)(q−1)θN(t). The q − 1 conjugates in the relative norm all have this same residue for the corresponding t. Principal-ideal congruence[2135] · Residues of conjugates and their qth powers[2136] · The relative norm in the residue computation[2137]
  3. For the general 𝔞′ in the application, take P in the inverse class and write P𝔞′ = (y). At any prime above q, write A for the upper principal solution, B for the twisted lower principal solution, and z for the twisted image of X. The two preceding comparisons give A ≡ B and A/X′ ≡ ξ B/z. All entries are units at this place. Cancelling gives X′ ≡ ξ−1z. The one root ξc = ξ−1 works at every such place and satisfies ξc2qN = 1. Fix the selected rational prime r ≡ 1 modulo F. Restricting one place over r to the two cyclotomic fields gives the prime ideals v and v′ used to construct Xd and Xqd. To apply both comparisons to the upper ideal v′ we need a lower generator for Norm(v′). The relative residue degree tells us which power of Xd to take. Which degree counts the conjugates, and which degree counts the ideal?

Put N = Fd and enlarge the level to qN by a fresh prime q coprime to N. The construction chooses its two cyclotomic fields inside one algebraic closure. Even if the two embeddings were initially chosen separately, every Nth root of unity is a power of a primitive root of order qN. This puts the smaller field inside the larger one in precisely one way compatible with the chosen embeddings. Restricting the same place above the rational prime r then gives primes 𝔭′ above 𝔭. Comparing the two embeddings[2146] Restricting the selected place[2143]

The field norm counts conjugates. A relative automorphism fixes the roots of order N and can act by any nonzero residue on a primitive qth root. Indeed, for a generator g modulo q, the Chinese remainder theorem gives an exponent equal to 1 modulo N and to g modulo q. The resulting power map on roots gives an automorphism τ of KqN over KN. Its first q − 1 powers are distinct on the primitive qth root. They exhaust the relative Galois group since the degree is φ(qN)/φ(N) = q − 1, where φ counts invertible residues. Hence the product of τi(Xqd) for 0 ≤ i < q − 1 is its field norm. The relative degree[2147] The exponent on the two sets of roots[2148] All the conjugates in the norm[2149]

The ideal norm counts residue-field degree. For r ∤ qN, write ordn(r) for the least positive k with rk ≡ 1 modulo n. At either level the prime is unramified, and Frobenius acts on the roots by the rth power. Its order is the absolute residue degree. Write κ(𝔭) for the residue field at 𝔭. Degrees multiply in the tower of residue fields, giving

s = [κ(𝔭′) : κ(𝔭)] = ordqN(r) / ordN(r),   Norm(𝔭′) = 𝔭s.

Thus Xds satisfies the two generator conditions for Norm(𝔭′). Raising to the power s multiplies each ideal exponent by s and preserves the identity with complex conjugation. This explains its exponent in both the norm formula and the congruence. The denominator in the norm formula uses the inverse of the qth-power action on the lower roots. The admissible auxiliary primes have orders of r prime to ℓ, and r ≡ 1 modulo F. By the Chinese remainder theorem their least common multiple is ordqN(r), so ℓ ∤ s. Residue degrees and the prime-ideal norm[2140] A prime-to-ℓ exponent[2150] Using the same lower power in the residue comparison[2144]

Check the two norms at levels 21 and 273

Take F = ℓ = 3, d = 7, q = 13 and r = 307. Both auxiliary primes are 1 modulo 3. Modulo 3, 7 and 13 the residues of 307 are 1, −1 and 8, of orders 1, 2 and 4 respectively (8² ≡ −1 modulo 13). The absolute residue degrees at levels 21 and 273 are therefore 2 and 4. The relative ideal norm is 𝔭². The residue field at 𝔭′ has 307⁴ elements and (307²)² = 307⁴. On elements the relative norm has twelve factors. For a primitive thirteenth root ζ these give Norm(1 − ζ) = ∏j=112(1 − ζj) = 13 by evaluating 1 + T + ⋯ + T12 at 1. Here 3 divides the number of conjugates and is coprime to the exponent 2 needed for the next normalization.

Both comparisons now use the same exponent s, prime to ℓ. The norm identity has a root factor of order dividing 2N. The congruence uses one root at all places over q, of order dividing 2qN. The two roots may differ. Their common order bound 2qN lets the next normalization remove each root, giving a norm identity and congruence with exponent qs.

8.24Why the Bernoulli factor is integral

To combine several primes in the minus estimate, the proof discards some character factors from an ℓ-adic product. This step is safe when each discarded factor has nonnegative valuation. Where does that integrality come from? At twist j put k = j + 1 ≥ 2. If χ has level N, conductor f and primitive character χ*, its denominator-cleared Bernoulli value is α = NPkBk,χ*, where Pk is the product of the primes at most k + 1. The two integer multipliers pay for different denominators. Normalization and conductor[1982] Use of integrality in the valuation sum[2151]

Expand the Bernoulli polynomial in ordinary Bernoulli numbers Bh. The rational coefficient attached to one residue a is

fk−1Bk(a/f) = ∑h=0k binom(k,h) Bh fh−1ak−h.

At h = 0 the factor f−1 can introduce a conductor denominator. Multiplying the entire sum by f changes every exponent to the nonnegative integer h. For a positive even h, the von Staudt–Clausen formula expresses Bh as an integer minus a sum of 1/p over primes with p−1 dividing h. Each such p is at most h+1 ≤ k+1, so it divides Pk. The remaining indices give B₀ = 1, B₁ = −½ and Bh = 0 for odd h > 1. Thus PkBh is integral throughout, and fPk times the displayed coefficient is an integer, residue by residue. Polynomial expansion at a rational point[2152] Common denominator for ordinary Bernoulli numbers[2153] Termwise integer formula[2154]

Multiplying these integers by χ*(a) and summing keeps the result in the ring generated by the character values. A unit value is a root of unity, hence an algebraic integer, and a nonunit contributes zero. Each unit modulo f lifts to a unit modulo N, so the values of χ* belong to the ring generated by the original χ. Finally f divides N. Multiplying by the integer N/f proves the required integrality of α in that ring. Integer-weighted character sum[2155] Integrality of unit values[2156] Lifting a unit from the conductor[2157] Integral closure and change of level[2158]

The same scaling also allows a single archimedean bound. For k ≥ 2 the Fourier expansion on [0,1] pairs the positive and negative frequencies. Each pair of unit complex phases has absolute value at most 2. Its reciprocal-power sum is bounded by 2∑m≥11/m² = π²/3 < 4. Consequently |Bk(x)| ≤ 4k!/(2π)k. There are f terms in the primitive sum, each carrying fk−1 and a character value of absolute value at most 1. Using f ≤ N, Pk ≤ 4k+1 and 4/(2π) ≤ 1 gives |α| ≤ 16Nk+1k!. The formal proof imports von Staudt–Clausen, the Bernoulli Fourier series, the sum of reciprocal squares and the primorial estimate at precisely these steps. Paired Fourier modes[2159] Uniform bound on the polynomial[2160] Summation over the conductor[2161] Primorial estimate and the factor 16[1985]

An odd character of conductor three

For j = 2, k = 3. Choose the quadratic character modulo 3, with values 1, −1, 0 on 1, 2, 3. It has the required odd parity. Since B₃(x) = x³ − 3x²/2 + x/2, its values at ⅓ and ⅔ are 1/27 and −1/27. Hence

B3,χ* = 3²(1/27 + 1/27) = 2/3,   L(−2,χ*) = −2/9,   α = (3·2·3)(2/3) = 12.

At ℓ = 3 this factor contributes log 3 to the upper bound from valuations. At every odd prime exceeding 3 it contributes zero. The source first proves 1000 log log H + C from the zero-free box and then uses log H ≤ 3Yε/5(log Y)². The leading coefficient in units of log Y is at most 1000/(5 · 52) = 50/13 < 4, so the log log Y and constant terms fit in the remaining margin for large Y. The proof inputs at this point are the relative prime-number theorem in progressions with its exceptional-zero bound, primitive-character zero density, the quadratic-twist mean-square theorem and the contour tail estimates. Assigning each nontrivial twist to its selection[2264] Logarithmic derivative from the zero-free box[2265] The final coefficient four[2266] The three conclusions for the chosen primes[2267]

8.30How an interval with exponent two gives one with exponent three halves

Here a change of scale serves two constraints at once. Fix the character ψ, 0 < ε < 1/52 and a scale multiplier c ≥ 1. In addition to the cohomological window, assume the prime-pair existence input PairEx. It supplies primes meeting the size and divisibility requirements, coprime to the character modulus. For the indicated nontrivial quadratic twists it also supplies centered-sum and logarithmic-derivative bounds, and for the indicated real characters a zero-free rectangle. These are stronger assumptions than prime existence alone. Analytic requirements on a prime pair[2268]

At input scale Y0 the primes satisfy q ≡ 3 mod 8 and d ≡ 7 mod 16. Put A = Y0ε/5. Then A/2 < log q ≤ A and ½A(log Y0)² < log d ≤ A(log Y0)². The integer d + 1 is divisible by q and by every odd prime ≤ A. The auxiliary field is selected by the fixed subgroup described above. Congruence and scale restrictions[2269]

Write r = 2 + 8ε and b = c1/r. Choose the tower exponent function e using the fact that some power of two lies between z and 2z for z ≥ 1. Apply VWinAt to this function, obtaining J and a threshold. To place the output interval beyond a prescribed lower bound, choose X so large that X1/J exceeds that lower bound, the prime-pair threshold, b³ and b400. Choose the primes at X1/J, then take the cohomological window [W, W²] with W ≥ X1/J and W² ≤ X.

Set Z = bW. Since W ≥ b³, Z3/2 ≤ W². For every x ∈ [Z, Z3/2] set x′ = x/b. Both x′ and x are in [W, W²]. Evaluating the page rule at x′ gives xr ≤ c2e(x′) ≤ 2xr. Evaluating the cohomological bound at that same x′ supplies its field at exactly that same tower level. Since x′ ≥ b400, we have

x400 = b400(x′)400 ≤ (x′)401,   exp((x′)ε/2) ≤ exp(xε/2).

All summands in the cohomological sum are nonnegative. Shortening the twist range and increasing the allowed upper bound therefore gives the bound required by WinDatum. The loss of one power from 401 to 400 pays for rescaling. Within a chosen window the primes can stay fixed, while the tower index depends on the point of evaluation. Order of choices[2270] Rescaling and twist cutoff[2271] Output window data[2272]

8.31From finite subsets of primes to a series

The arithmetic comparison eventually needs a summable sequence of nonnegative terms. Choose the algebraic closure and local data attached to the arithmetic datum. Finiteness of each module length ensures conversion from extended natural numbers to integers recovers its value. For each prime the arithmetic contribution is bounded by its logarithm times the sum of these lengths in the specified range. All finite subsums are bounded by the same B. Their supremum is therefore finite, and equals the sum of the full nonnegative series. This is the use of the universal quantifier over finite sets of primes. The resulting package also keeps the finiteness assertion on the relevant twists. Reading the cohomological estimate into the arithmetic data[2273]

Why is an exponential bound small enough for a final estimate near √x? At the same scale x the weight in a single arithmetic measurement is b = exp(xε). The cohomological series has sum at most exp(xε/2) = √b. Since b ≥ 1, it fits within the allowance b in the finite-place lattice estimate. This is a bound on one input to the measurement. Only after the arithmetic comparisons are added does the proof divide the error by the total weight to bound the centered prime sum. Where the series enters the lattice bound[2274] Absorbing its square-root allowance at the same scale[2275]

Turning this bound into the final divisible-lattice estimate also requires rank equalities, the local-to-global normalization and common family parameters. The preceding sections explain how the tower bounds, degree-two estimate and signed character counts apply to the same pair and field. The two-stage prime selection supplies the smoothed-sum and zero-free conditions for the same pair. The remaining interfaces there are the underlying progression, zero-density, mean-square and contour estimates. Use of the cohomological and geometric inputs[2276]

9The one-sided window theorem

Suppose the arithmetic argument repeatedly finds a stretch of scales on which a centered prime sum stays below a small power of the scale. A zero of an associated L-function would force a pole of its transform. How can a bound on scattered stretches rule out even one pole? High derivatives let us choose where the integral sees the function.

9.1The hypothesis in logarithmic coordinates

Fix 0 < θ < 1 and δ > 0. Write g(u) = GF(exp u) for a real weighted sum from a finite character family F. The abstract theorem below allows any real measurable g with |g(u)| ≤ C0 exp(2u) for u ≥ 0. Its transform Φ(s) agrees with ∫0∞ g(u) exp(−su) du for Re s > 2. Assume it extends holomorphically in the right half-plane outside a set Z of simple poles, every one of which has positive real part. Every point of the half-plane must have a punctured neighborhood free of Z, including points outside Z. At each pole the residue is nonzero, and at each real pole it is real and strictly positive. These assumptions comprise PoleData. Transform and pole hypotheses[2277]

Put U = log Y. Then [Y, Y1+δ] becomes I = [U, (1 + δ)U]. For every η > 0 and every lower limit U0, suppose there exist U ≥ U0 and a majorant R on I with R ≥ max(g, 0), such that R(u) exp(−θu) is integrable there and

∫I R(u) exp(−θu) du ≤ exp(ηU).

Theorem. Every ρ ∈ Z satisfies Re ρ ≤ θ. The window and its majorant may depend on η and U0. Between windows the growth estimate still holds. An arithmetic upper bound GF(y) ≤ C yθ on arbitrarily distant windows suffices. Take R(u) = |C| exp(θu). Its weighted integral equals |C|δU, which is at most exp(ηU) once U is large. From power bounds to the window hypothesis[2278] One-sided window theorem[2279]

Test the hypothesis on a single pole. Take θ = ½, δ = ½ and g(u) = exp(¾u). Its Laplace transform is 1/(s − ¾). On [U,3U/2] even the smallest admissible majorant has weighted integral 4(exp(3U/8) − exp(U/4)). For η = ⅛ this eventually exceeds exp(ηU) on every window. Change the sign of g and R = 0 works on every window, although the transform still has a pole at ¾. Its residue is now −1. This example explains the sign hypothesis at real poles and why the arithmetic only needs an upper bound.

9.2Choosing a derivative that sees the window

For Re z = σ > 2, define Ak(z) = (−1)kΦ(k)(z)/k!. In a small neighborhood with Re z ≥ 2 + α, α > 0, the differentiated integrand is bounded by C0uk exp(−αu), an integrable function. Repeated differentiation under the integral therefore gives

Ak(σ + iγ) = ∫0∞ g(u) exp(−iγu) Kk,σ(u) du,   Kk,a(u) = ukexp(−au)/k!.

This nonnegative kernel has its maximum at u = k/a for k > 0. Its integral is a−k−1, by substitution and integration by parts. The term g itself may change sign. Adding Re Ak(σ) to the triangle inequality for |Ak(σ + iγ)| replaces |g| by |g| + g = 2 max(g, 0). On I, use this majorant and the inequality vk/k! ≤ exp(v) at v = (σ − θ)u. Off I, use the growth bound. The result is

|Ak(σ + iγ)| + Re Ak(σ) ≤ 2 exp(ηU)/(σ − θ)k + 2C0 ∫(0,∞) ∖ I Kk,σ−2(u) du.

The real derivative acts as a correction for sign. Write g = g+ − g−, both parts nonnegative. The triangle inequality at σ + iγ counts both with a plus sign. At the real center, Ak(σ) = ∫(g+ − g−)K. Adding cancels the entire negative part and leaves at most 2∫g+K. The same derivative order must therefore work at both centers.

The integrand in this tail contains σ − 2 because |g| can grow as exp(2u). Estimating the tails of Kk,σ alone would lose that factor. Derivative identity[2280] One-sided derivative estimate[2281]

9.3A uniform estimate for the tails

For s > λ ≥ 0 and V = (1 + δ)U, multiply the integrand on u > V by exp(λ(u − V)), and on u < U by exp(λ(U − u)). Both multipliers are at least one in their respective regions. Extending the resulting integrals over the positive half-line gives

∫(0,∞) ∖ I Kk,s ≤ exp(−λV)/(s − λ)k+1 + exp(λU)/(s + λ)k+1.

The source makes concrete choices depending first on δ and then on the window. Take λ = 2 + 6/δ, M = λ(1 + δ), σ = M(2 + λ), s = σ − 2, and k = ⌈(1 + δ/2)σU⌉. For U ≥ 1 we have k ≥ U and s > λ. To bound the first term after multiplication by σk, set a = s − λ. The inequality log(σ/a) ≤ (σ − a)/a = 1/(M − 1), together with (1 + δ/2)σ = M(M − 1), gives −λV + k log(σ/a) ≤ 1. Its contribution is at most exp(1)/a.

For the second term set b = s + λ. Then log(σ/b) ≤ −(λ − 2)/b. Since (1 + δ/2)(λ − 2) = λ + 1 and λ(σ − 2 + λ) ≤ (λ + 1)σ, the lower bound on k gives λU − k(λ − 2)/b ≤ 0. Therefore this contribution is at most 1/b. Both bounds are independent of the chosen window. Combining with the preceding inequality gives a constant C1 such that, for every η > 0 and arbitrarily large U, some integer k ≥ U satisfies simultaneously for every real γ

Locate one of the kernels numerically

Take δ = 1 and U = 10. The source’s choices give λ = 8, M = 16, σ = 160 and k = 2400. The known interval is [10,20], and K2400,160 peaks at 15. Even the kernel after the growth correction peaks at 2400/158 ≈ 15.19. For fixed δ and growing U, how wide is a kernel compared with the interval? Normalizing Kk,a to have integral one gives mean (k + 1)/a and variance (k + 1)/a². Both follow by taking its first two moments with the integral formula above. Thus its standard deviation grows like √U, while the window’s width grows like U. The exponential tail inequalities give the stronger rate needed for the pole argument.

|Ak(σ + iγ)| + Re Ak(σ) ≤ C1 exp(ηU)/(σ − θ)k.

The order k can change each time the arithmetic supplies a new window. Exponential tilting[2282] Choice of scale and order[2283] Quantifiers in the derivative bound[2284]

9.4Isolating the pole seen by the derivatives

Suppose a pole has real part greater than θ. All poles lie to the left of σ because the Laplace integral is holomorphic on Re s > 2. Write E = σ − θ. The closed disk of radius E about σ lies in Re s ≥ θ > 0, so it contains finitely many poles by compactness and the punctured-neighborhood assumption. If it contains no poles, take D = E. The hypothesized pole then has horizontal distance strictly less than D and gives the first case below. Otherwise let D be the distance from σ to a nearest pole in the disk. In both cases the open disk of radius D is pole-free.

If a pole ρ1 has σ − Re ρ1 < D, then a disk of radius D centered at σ + i Im ρ1 contains it. Move that center by a sufficiently small vertical amount. Only finitely many poles in a slightly enlarged disk matter, and two distinct poles equally far from the moving center can tie at at most one height. Indeed their squared distances have a difference affine in the height. For equal imaginary parts the equality would also require equal real parts, since both poles lie to the left of σ. Avoiding the finitely many ties gives a center z = σ + iγ with a unique nearest pole ρ at distance d < D. Choose a radius r with d < r ≤ D isolating this pole.

In the other case all horizontal distances σ − Re ρ are at least D. There must be a nearest pole in the disk because the hypothesized pole has horizontal distance less than E. For any nearest pole the Euclidean distance D is at least its horizontal distance, now at least D. Equality forces the imaginary part to vanish. This identifies one real pole β = σ − D > θ. Every other pole in the finite disk is strictly farther away. Choose r with D < r ≤ E isolating β. Geometry at the real center[2285] Perturbing the height[2286]

9.5Two incompatible derivative rates

In the first case subtract c/(s − ρ), where c is the nonzero residue. Its subtraction leaves a holomorphic function on the disk after filling the removable value at ρ. For R = (d + r)/2, Cauchy's estimate on the circle of radius R gives

|Ak(z) − c/(z − ρ)k+1| ≤ M1/Rk.

The real center also has a pole-free disk of radius D > R, so |Ak(σ)| ≤ M2/Rk. Substituting these estimates into the upper bound for the derivatives yields

(|c|/d) d−k ≤ (M1 + M2) R−k + C1 exp(ηU) E−k.

For a numerical reading of the last step, suppose d = 2, R = 3 and E = 4. With η = ½ log(3/2), multiplying by 2k leaves a first error proportional to (2/3)k. Since U ≤ k, the window error is at most a constant times (√(3/2)/2)k. Both tend to zero, however sparsely the integers k occur, while the residue contributes |c|/2 every time. The inequalities below apply the same comparison to the actual radii.

Choose 0 < η < log(R/d). Multiply the inequality by dk. Because U ≤ k and E ≥ R > d, the right side tends to zero along the chosen windows. The left side is a fixed positive number.

In the real-pole case take d = σ − β. At the real center the pole contributes c/dk+1 to Ak(σ) with real c > 0. Cauchy's estimate bounds the remainder by M1/Rk for R = (d + r)/2. The nonnegative absolute-value term in the derivative bound can be dropped. The same rate contradiction follows. A negative real residue would reverse the critical sign, which explains the positivity requirement in PoleData. Subtracting the polar part[2287] Two-center argument[2288] Real-pole argument[2289]

9.6Choosing the exponent after choosing the alleged zero

Let β > 1/2 be the real part being tested. Pick h = ½ min(β − 1/2, 1/2) and θ = 1/2 + h. This ensures θ < min(β,1). Fix a level containing a retained character with the alleged zero. The associated Dirichlet characters, their weights and the function tested for poles are now fixed. The arithmetic construction supplies eD, eL and ε1 > 0 before ε is chosen. Set C = eD + eL + 7 and take ε = min(ε1/2, h/(|C| + 1)). Then Cε ≤ h. Choose the auxiliary arithmetic data for this ε and their large-scale threshold, then choose windows beyond that threshold and beyond 1. These data supply a bound for the weighted sum at the level already fixed. On those windows, the arithmetic exponent can be increased to θ. The theorem excludes a family pole with real part β. For the concrete analytic family, the proof also invokes known nonvanishing at Re s ≥ 1 and uses its pole construction for the remaining open strip. Order of parameter choices[2290] From the level to the character family[2291] Return to L-functions[29]

9.7A zero at 0.60 and the interval that excludes it

Fix the character family that sees the zero, as in the opening example. With θ = 0.55, choose ε ≤ 0.005 within the arithmetic threshold. The specialized estimate gives ½ + 9ε ≤ 0.545. For any prescribed lower cutoff, the arithmetic construction supplies an interval [Z, Z3/2] beyond it. At every point there, the fixed family sum is at most x0.55. Put U = log Z. The function R(u) = exp(0.55u) bounds the positive part on [U, 3U/2]. Multiplication by exp(−0.55u) leaves the constant one. Its integral is U/2, at most exp(ηU) once U is large, for every prescribed η > 0. The window theorem now bounds every pole of this family by 0.55 in real part. A pole at 0.60 contradicts that conclusion.

10Reflection and the final statement

Once every Dirichlet character has a zero-free right half-plane, the passage to classical RH is short. Two small points do most of the work. A change of modulus introduces finite Euler factors, and reflection changes the character.

10.1Removing an imprimitive level

The conductor f of χ modulo N is the least divisor through which its character on units factors. Write ψ for the primitive character at that conductor. Changing to modulus N suppresses Euler factors at primes dividing N. On the common domain of the change-of-level identity, this gives

L(s,χ) = L(s,ψ) ∏p∣N (1 − ψ(p) p−s).

For a prime dividing f, ψ(p) = 0 and the displayed factor equals one. For every other prime its absolute value before subtraction satisfies |ψ(p) p−s| ≤ p−Re s < 1 whenever Re s > 0. Each factor is therefore nonzero. The formula initially follows from Euler products and extends where the continued identity applies. The formal change-of-level lemma asks that ψ be nonprincipal or s ≠ 1. If χ is nonprincipal then ψ must be nonprincipal too, since inducing a principal character would give χ principal. Thus the exception χ = 1 and s = 1 is accounted for. From primitive to all characters[2292]

A change of modulus you can calculate. Let ψ be the character modulo 3 that takes −1 at 2. Induce it to χ modulo 6. On the odd integers the two agree, and the change removes the even terms. Thus L(s,χ) = (1 + 2−s)L(s,ψ). The factor at 3 is one because ψ(3) = 0. When Re s > 0, the added term 2−s has absolute value strictly below one. At the boundary point s = πi/log 2 it equals −1 and the finite factor vanishes. This locates precisely where the zero-transfer argument uses strict positivity of the real part.

10.2The strip theorem for characters

Assume 0 < Re s < 1 and L(s,χ) = 0. The finite factors transfer the zero to ψ. Its completed function is obtained by multiplying by the real gamma factor appropriate to the parity of ψ. The gamma arguments have positive real part in this strip, so the factors are finite and nonzero. In particular the completed function vanishes too. The functional equation for ψ−1, evaluated at s, gives a zero of the completed function for ψ−1 at 1 − s. On units the inverse character is its complex conjugate. The arguments s and 1 − s avoid 0 and 1. Returning to the uncompleted function gives L(1 − s, ψ−1) = 0.

If Re s < ½, then Re(1 − s) > ½, contradicting right-half-plane nonvanishing for the inverse primitive character. If Re s > ½, nonvanishing for χ already contradicts the original zero. This leaves Re s = ½. It proves the strip statement for arbitrary moduli. Primitive transfer, reflection and strip conclusion[2293]

Follow a hypothetical zero of a complex character

Modulo 5, the residue 2 generates the unit group. The rule ψ(2) = i therefore fixes a primitive character and ψ−1(2) = −i. If L(¼ + 2i,ψ) vanished, the completed functional equation would give a zero for ψ−1 at ¾ − 2i. The modulus is still 5. The character has changed, so the right-half-plane theorem must cover the inverse as well. Conjugating this latter zero would give a zero for ψ at ¾ + 2i. This last operation explains why the same-character symmetry in a plot is a reflection across a vertical line, even though the functional equation uses 1 − s.

10.3Why classical RH excludes the negative even integers

The public zeta theorem follows a slightly different route. Specialize right-half-plane nonvanishing to the unique character of modulus one. Suppose ζ(s) = 0 with s ≠ 1 and s outside the negative even integers. The right-hand case is impossible immediately. For Re s < ½, put w = 1 − s. Since ζ(0) = −½, s ≠ 0 and w ≠ 1. We have Re w > ½, so ζ(w) ≠ 0, and w avoids all nonpositive integers. In the normalization used by this source the functional equation reads

ζ(1−w) = 2(2π)−w Γ(w) cos(πw/2) ζ(w).

The power of 2π is nonzero and Γ has no zero for Re w > 0. If the cosine vanished, w would be an odd integer, so s would be even. Positive even integers contradict Re s < ½, zero has already been excluded, and negative even integers are exactly the excluded trivial zeros. Every factor on the right is therefore nonzero, contradicting ζ(s) = 0. This proves the implication from the nonvanishing input to the exact classical target. Classical reflection proof[2294] Modulus-one specialization[6]

Why can the same argument accommodate ζ(−2) and ζ(0)?

For s = −2 one has w = 3. The gamma and zeta factors on the right are finite and nonzero, but cos(3π/2) = 0. The equation gives ζ(−2) = 0. For s = 0 one has w = 1. Now the cosine vanishes while ζ(w) has a pole, so value-by-value multiplication at w = 1 is unavailable. Writing w = 1 + h, cos(πw/2) = −πh/2 + O(h³) and ζ(w) = 1/h + O(1). Their product tends to −π/2. The remaining multiplier tends to 2(2π)−1Γ(1) = 1/π. This recovers ζ(0) = −½.
